utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to one and all. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Having said this, this is Thursday, the 6th of July, 2006. We're going to be working until 1.45 today. Without further ado and wasting time, I'm going to give the floor to the first of the Defence counsel who are going to start the cross-examination. Who will it be? Counsel Alaburic or Nozica, which one is it? Mrs. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My colleague Nozica will begin the cross-examination, but in order to protect the interests of my client, I'd like to say the following: In today's short working day we have to get through the cross-examination by four Defence teams and must leave enough time to our colleague Mr. Scott for additional questions. I know that the Bench might have more questions as well, and then time is needed for the introduction of exhibits. I'd just like to emphasise that this kind of stage management is not the consequence of -- or any fault of the Defence team and is not the result of the agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Manolic. My name is Senka Nozica, a lawyer from Sarajevo, and I'm going to ask you questions today on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Bruno Stojic. Yesterday, we had a little problem with the transcript and the interpretation because we were too fast. We speak the same language, and we understand each other, but would you please try and slow down.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you to adhere to that. In your testimony, several times so far you told us that you did not agree with the policy waged at a given period of time by the Croatian Republic, or Croatian state, on three points: The relationship towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not agree with the functioning of -- or lack of functioning of state -- by the rule of law, and you had some inter-party disputes as to the way problems should be solved. Yesterday, you told us something very important, and I would like to confirm that, which will help us in our job - me too, you too - that your disagreement in fact with the policy waged by Croatia towards Herceg-Bosna or, rather, Bosnia in general and the policy waged by the Croats in Bosnia in fact emerged at the point of time when the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we, for the transcript, for the record, give a time frame for that? When was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in the transcripts you will find the dates that Herceg-Bosna was established as a republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm of course well aware of that, but I'd like to hear from you. When do you think that was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you give us the month, perhaps, and the day, the month?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was autumn, sometime in autumn. Perhaps the 9th or, rather, perhaps September or October, I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I'd now like to go on to discuss the transcripts that you have been referring to for three days now, and I'd like to take a look at where you agree and disagree with some of the positions put forward by the state council at the sessions they held. I don't think we'll need to have the documents appear on the monitor, on our screens again, except perhaps in some exceptions when I wish to refer to certain paragraphs, but I'm going to rely on your very good memory, and I'm sure you'll remember --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't overestimate my memory, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, sir, yesterday after your presentation and your testimony over the past three days, I value your memory very highly. I have good reason to do so, and I'm sure you will remember all the things I'm going to talk about, but let's start with the first session. The first session was held on the 8th of June, 1991, let me remind you. It was in fact the time when the president informed you about the results of the conclusions of the Presidency of the SFRY, the Yugoslav state Presidency, and that was still the time when Croatia was very much taken up with how to settle accounts and with the remains of Yugoslavia, and so on, and when Bosnia-Herzegovina was mentioned in that context only insofar as that was important for Croatian policy.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to emphasise that that was the period when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia still existed, with all its legal apparatus, the constitution, and other provisions. So we had to take care and take into account all these elements not to come into conflict and not to be accused of toppling that system.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to speak up, please, or into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you agree that you didn't actually discuss that item?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next session, and that next session is the one of the 26th session of the Supreme State Council, held on the 12th of November, 1991, and here too we have a topic discussed under number 2 of the agenda and that -- or it is Prosecution Exhibit, in fact, 00068 where the deepening of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina was discussed once again. The Serbs were holding a referendum at that time, and you did not have any discussions with respect to that issue and those questions belong to the time frame that you've just explained to us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. At a meeting of the 18th of November, 1991, and that is Exhibit P 00080, under Miscellaneous, I think that it was an important session because of issues related to Bosnia-Herzegovina. As I was saying, under Others, or Miscellaneous, President Tudjman informed you about a piece of information received according to which the Western Herzegovina Travnik region would gain their declaration to set up a joint Herceg-Bosna; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as I was able to go through that, you never had any dilemmas or questions with respect to what was discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not at that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Would you explain to me, when you say perhaps not at the meeting or at the session certainly not, but why did you say just at the meeting not? Did you have any queries otherwise?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was discussed previously and afterwards as well, whether in a broader circle or narrower circle of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, but regardless of this, everything that you discussed was not as drastic for it to merit for you to intervene at the session in any way.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at the way in which the meeting was chaired with the president's authority, I don't think that was necessary, and I wouldn't think that that would have been useful, to open up a debate of that kind, although it was quite clear to one and all what the position was and what the creation of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna created.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You bring me to a dilemma now. Actually, I'm not able to draw the proper conclusion about your testimony now. I'm in a quandary. Yesterday you said and repeated today that with respect to Herceg-Bosna, regardless of whether it was called a community or not or republic or not, your first opposition there was to the policy when the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So can I conclude that you weren't opposed to anything at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point in time during the session, and on the basis of the transcripts, that is not evident. However, I remained firm in my position that the formation of Herceg-Bosna was a question that had to have some attributes of statehood which would then collide with the existing Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, we're going discuss that after the autumn of 1993. We'll get to that in due course, when you say you were opposed to what was going on, but let me now remind you of something else and ask you whether you attended the meeting of the 27th of December, 1991, and that was the meeting attended by Mr. Kljuic. And I'd like e-court, please, and Prosecution Exhibit P 00088 to be placed on the screens, and I'd like to remind you it was a meeting, as I say, attended by Mr. Kljuic. He came in to present his position, and the other Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina came too, and there was discussion there about the positions of Mr. Kljuic as opposed to the positions presented by the others who attended. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date of the session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The 27th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but you have it in the transcripts whether I was present or not, and I will believe you when you tell me and I'll believe the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will show you the transcript, that's why we insisted upon it, because for some sessions we do have a list of those present but for others, unfortunately, we do not have a list of those who attended, so I cannot establish that myself and that's why I'm asking you whether you were there or not. May we have the agenda on our screens, please. Scroll down a little, please. Up. May we have page 2 on the screen now, please. Can you see that and read it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The meeting was a very important political one and stood out, and I'm sure you would have remembered it had you been present, but I have my reasons for thinking that you weren't present. Mate Boban was present, for example, Mr. Brkic, and a large number of Croats, as you said, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the meeting at which Mr. Kljuic stood up in opposition to certain positions presented by others.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the contents, and based on what I've read here, I don't remember having attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was asked because the Prosecutor, in the summary that he provided us with about your testimony, said that you were at that meeting on the 27th of December, 1991, and that you would confirm that, confirm what happened at the meeting. You don't remember, but do you exclude the possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't exclude the possibility of my having been there. I would have to read the transcript quietly and concentrate on that very -- in order to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May I try and jog your memory? Do you remember the debate in general when Mr. Kljuic was there and Mr. Kostroman was there and when the other Croats were there and when the decisions were read out on the establishment of the Community of Herceg-Bosna? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I remember a meeting of that kind attended by Kljuic and the other people that you mentioned, but I can't claim that that was that very session. I think there were a number of meetings that were held to which Kljuic came.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, for the transcript, I'd just like to underline that you leave the possibility open that you might have been at the meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Based on the contents and the participants, I might have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't have you taking the floor, being recorded as having taken the floor at the meeting, so it's difficult to establish.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's why I have my doubts whether I actually attended or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like to refer now to another meeting. Let's have a look at the meeting of the 10th of March, 1992, and it is Prosecution Exhibit 000134, a meeting where you did not take part in the debate on the item of the agenda, on the work of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina and our links with them. That was a meeting where my client is mentioned, and let me remind you it is the meeting where Mate Boban provided information about the procurement of the Golf cars. Do you remember what Mr. Bruno Stojic did at that time? And we're talking about the 10th of March, 1992. What positions he held and how he was able to procure those Golf cars.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what posts the individuals mentioned occupied except for Kljuic. I know he was president. Except for Brkic. I know that he was to take over the office of president. I remember that. However, the other positions and who held them, I really can't know. I didn't enter into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At that time, the material time referred to by Mr. Boban, Mr. Bruno Stojic worked as assistant in the Ministry of the Internal Affairs or, rather, deputy. I was not precise enough. He was deputy in the Internal Ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it's not a Herzegovina structure, it was a post in the official state. And since you, in response to a question from the Prosecution, speculated and said that those Golf cars were perhaps procured from the factory, I'm going to ask you whether you would agree with me when I tell you that the position of Mr. Bruno Stojic was such at that time that he was able to procure all equipment for all the police stations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that, as such, performing that function, that's how those Golf cars were procured.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that because I don't know which position he occupied. The Ministry of the Interior, I know what that structure was. I know that there were a number of assistant ministers. I don't know whether Mr. Prlic -- Stojic -- yes, Stojic, I beg your pardon, was in that particular department for procuring equipment or whether he was something else. So I really can't answer the question. I don't know what post he occupied, so I can't give you an affirmative answer or a negative answer, but the fact is that at the session the figure bandied about was that of 150 Golf cars procured.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to say that you were commenting on something you don't know about and that is that those Golfs were procured for the requirements of the police of the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that that is how -- a certain number of those cars came to the area that they were talking about, Mr. Boban mentioned. I just wanted to highlight that, because you said something and speculated on something that you didn't know directly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know directly what was stated at the meeting, and Boban did state the figure of 150 Golf cars as procured by that man, he said that at that session. So I'm adhering to that text and you can stick to that too and we'll explain the situation very easily if we do that. If you have any other knowledge, that's another matter. I can't enter into anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you thought that these were Golf cars that were procured from the factory, so you were talking about something you didn't know first-hand. That is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're dealing with 150 Golf cars, then the assumption must be where did they come from? Where did those Golf cars come from? And that is why I speculated and guessed, and as I knew that there was a Golf factory in Sarajevo, I logically concluded that there could have been 150 new Golf cars coming from that factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to turn to the session held on the 3rd of November, 1992, which is Exhibit 00699. And this is a session where Slavonski Brod -- no, I apologise, Bosanski Brod was discussed. So it was on the 3rd of November, 1992. Do you remember that session?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, if this is indeed the session where we discussed the withdrawal of Croatian army from the territory of Bosnian Posavina; and in relation to that, we discussed the destruction of the bridge, the issue of Brod, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And on the agenda there was an item, the report of the state commission on Bosanski Brod. You were quite active in that session, although I have to say that there were many -- that there were not many sessions where you were not quite talkative.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as is my habit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You spoke quite a lot about demobilisation, about that issue. The status of Croatian officials in the army was also discussed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to stick to the text. I think the text is more relevant than my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Other than this, there were no other topics discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we're not thinking of the same session. The session where the report was given about the withdrawal of our forces from Bosnian Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same session.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the commission, you said who was in that post, who gave the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let's turn to the session held on the 27th of January, 1993, and this seems to be the most problematic one. This is Prosecution Exhibit 01325. On the first day of your testimony, in direct examination you commented on some portions of this session, and then yesterday you said that you did not attend it. Let me remind you. On the first day, that was the 4th of July, transcript page 4433 until 4434, you said there that you attended the session.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is clear on the face of the minutes, because that document states the -- those present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas asked you about that session yesterday because, during that session, a letter of Mr. Prlic was read out. You said that you did not attend that session. Let us now clarify. Did you attend or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please show us the very beginning of the minutes. If it says that I was there, then I definitely did attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the first page of this minutes. So this is Exhibit P 01325.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th of January, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You'll see it on the screen and you can verify. Could we please see the next page so that the witness can see the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My name is not mentioned on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We don't know yet. We have two different accounts right now, one saying that you attended and one saying that you didn't. Can we see the agenda and a bit below the agenda so that the witness can see it. I think that that's quite important. It's below the Miscellaneous item or, rather, scroll down. Yes, this is good.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the people mentioned in these minutes, I think that this has more to do with operative issues than any political discussion of a problem. Based on the list of attendees, I would say that those were people from operative affairs; minister of the interior, his assistant, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When Mr. Karnavas ask you yesterday, you said, "I did not attend that session." I want to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying now. Looking at the minutes, I would say that I didn't attend that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. But on the first day, when examined by the Prosecutor, when he asked you about the report that Mr. Susak received from Kordic and Stojic, and when the Prosecutor referred you to the pages of these minutes -- this is ERN number 01867580. 01867580. So when asked then, you said that you knew about this. So how come you know about this? Is it because you attended this session or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I did not attend that session, but if you read me out the text of my evidence in chief, then I can perhaps clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, the text is before you, the upper portion. Another text we're interested, ERN 01867583.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See here, when it comes --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This portion. This portion. Would you please look at the first paragraph. When asked by the Prosecutor in your first day of evidence, you said that you knew about this. So how come you knew about this if you didn't attend this session?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible that I could have learned of this from other sources. Therefore, I can't tell you now firmly whether I attended that session or not, but most likely the minutes would have reflected had I been present. As to the problems presented by Gojko Susak, those problems were in place for quite a long time in that area, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, as the lines moved. So it was possible that I could have learned about this from other sources, other reports, just as the minutes reflect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that you didn't attend this session but that you learned of it from other sources?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can conclude that, because I fully believe the minutes in the portion where it lists the attendees. That was quite carefully recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, yesterday and the day before that, both when asked by Mr. Praljak and by my other colleagues, you said repeatedly that you could testify only about what was stated in the transcripts, and on a number of important issues you said that you had no other information. So based on this, I can conclude that in addition to what you learned during these sessions, you also had some other sources of information, especially when it comes to this issue, to Mr. Susak. Did he inform you about the contacts with people there Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a firm answer about that because there were very many sources of information in different periods of time. Now we are dealing with the events discussed at this session which most likely I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please understand me. Please don't feel offended.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not offended at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is extremely important for me, extremely important, because my client was mentioned here, and I have to insist on clarifying this issue. I have to know whether you attended that session or not. Did you receive the information at the session or via some other means?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This issue that is discussed here, I am familiar with that issue. Now, whether I attended that session, or perhaps I was late arriving and therefore my presence was not recorded, or I learned of this from other sources, and there were a whole number of those sources, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said to my colleague that you reviewed these transcripts before coming here; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't remember that you provided a very clear answer as to how come you had these transcripts available to you. Do you have them in your personal archive?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you're aware of the fact that these transcripts circulate throughout Zagreb in quite large copies, so it's not difficult to come by these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it's not difficult, and you had them.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had some. I can't say that I had all of them. And I had some minutes. I also had my notes from sessions, party meetings, definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you discuss with the Prosecutor specifically the report from this session that I'm referring to now? Did you discuss the reports sent by Kordic and Stojic on the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was put to me here, and I think that we did put the text that we are dealing with now -- I'm not quite sure, though, because a lot of texts were put here. I'm not sure whether this was put to me by the Prosecutor through his question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I didn't ask you about what was going on here in the courtroom. I asked you about your contact with the Prosecution before arriving here.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a minute. We mustn't overlap. Did you ever discuss with the Prosecution whether you knew that Susak received reports from Kordic and Stojic about the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not directly, except what one could learn through the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just saying this not because of your sake but because of the sake of the transcript. In the last summary we received from the Prosecution on the 28th of June, 1996, [as interpreted] that's precisely what is stated there; namely that you would testify about contacts and information that Susak received about the status or situation in Bosnia from Kordic and Stojic. This is why I was greatly surprised to hear from you yesterday that you did not attend the session at all. That's all I have to say about this session.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us deal with the contents, with the subject matter. You are focusing on the session alone. As to the reporting by Kordic and others, this is something that Susak received on a regular basis. So I can't focus on the text alone, on the text here. And that was quite a routine procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How do you know that Susak received these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this specific report; I just know that they reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How come you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because it was mentioned in many sessions, not just in one session of the Defence and National Security Council. Not just in one session, it was mentioned in almost all sessions when the topic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But now you just said that in this particular session -- I'm not interested in general -- things in general. I'm interested in specific things. You said that in this session, when specific names were mentioned - Kordic, Stojic, Petkovic - you were not present. Can we put an end to this discussion. I'm not asking you just about the session, I'm asking you about the contents.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm interested in the contents, not just the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I showed you the contents.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the contents, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. We can move to the next session. This is session 145 T -- Prosecution Exhibit 1452. This is 9th of February, 1993. Did you attend this session?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just see the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The date is the 9th of February, 1993. Could we see it in e-court, this exhibit. The first page is 01452. That's the first page.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 3, please. ERN number -- or, rather, 3 in Croatian. ERN number 01867533. If we can scroll down, please, with this portion beginning with, "As you know ..." I will remind you that this is the 9th of February, 1993, quite an important date. It deals with -- oh, yesterday, when speaking of supply of weapons to the Bosnian army, you said that it was mostly smuggling and that it couldn't have been a legal process. I will read this out carefully. "As you are aware, I was called by the president of Iran several days ago, Mr. Rafsanjani." These are the words of Mr. Tudjman. "And yesterday evening I received a call from the president of Turkey, from Washington, following the conversation with the US President Clinton. Both of them appealed to us to enable the supply of weapons to Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said to both of them that they should say to Izetbegovic that he needs to prevent conflicts with the Croats and that we, on our part, would do -- would do that, but that they need to prevent conflict with Croats and they need to achieve agreement with Croats. In relation to that, we have specific demands. Even the president of Turkey spoke of them yesterday. But otherwise, two helicopters were delivered to them and weaponry. I think that we must be firm about this request that Izetbegovic give a public statement, that he sign what he actually rejected." And we know what he rejected. We are referring to the 9th of February, 1993. He refused to sign the Vance-Owen Plan; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Because otherwise we would be making concessions to them and they are continuing with their attacks against Croatian settlements and Croatian units." Please, can we turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I this that this is quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It didn't say there we are making concessions or, rather, there was a letter missing, and it meant that we are letting it through, meaning the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Correct. That's the meaning, we are letting it through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need to give comment here. This is quite important. This has nothing to do with the weapons going from Croatia. No. This were the weapons that were coming from other sides and that needed to transit Croatia and to be let through into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, you spent a lot of time talking about how Croatia was under embargo, and if a country is under an embargo, then no weapons can cross its territory. You called all of this smuggling, trafficking, everything that showed -- that Mr. Kovacic showed to you. You said you knew nothing about that, and I'm trying to show now to you that you were officially present in that body for which you claimed operated legally the whole time and that this body discussed the supply of weapons to Bosnia-Herzegovina which, in a way, represented a violation of embargo, at least in relation to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to understand who requested this from us. It was the other countries, such as Iran and Turkey. They wanted us to let this through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't have too much time - I apologise, Mr. Manolic - but the violation of something, of a decision, a resolution, you can't violate anything like that even if some international powers want you to do so, so this is just an illustration of the fact that you discussed the matter. And that's it. I know that you always have an additional explanation, but this is an illustration. You have provided your additional explanation, but it doesn't change anything. So in February, 1993, two points are essential to note here: The Croatian state is sending, or letting through across its territory, weapons to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were deciding on that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have proof and evidence of that, that it was let through. You only have proof and evidence in the transcript that Croatia was asked to do that, whereas President Tudjman very resolutely stated, "I want you to say that you're going to stop attacking."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I do have proof and evidence of that, and as far as I'm concerned, that's important for me that you discussed the issue.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. We did discuss the issue, but that still is not proof and evidence that Croatia actually let the weapons through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you opposed to that happening at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happening? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, the president is speaking here, and he is saying that. He's saying how this is going to be done.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please read the text, because what you're saying is your interpretation of the text, whereas we have the text before us, we have President Tudjman's words in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, you read it out, then. I didn't interpret it, I was reading it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 01867533. That is the number of the page. And the Exhibit number 0142 -- 01452. This is part 2. May we return to the first page. We're -- that's it. Could we zoom in on that. Lower down, please. You weren't looking at the text when I read it out a moment ago. Do you want me to read it again and you can follow on the screen? Can I do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but please proceed in a proper manner. "As you know, several days ago the president of Iran -- prior to this the president of Iran called me, and last night the president of Turkey called me from Washington, after having talked to the president of the United States, Clinton, both of them urging us to enable --" so they are urging us to enable the supply of weapons to BH. "I told them both that they can tell Izetbegovic to present the conflict with the Croats and that we, for our part --" Well, what else did I say? That's precisely what I read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I had to interrupt you. I really don't have time. I do apologise, Mr. Manolic, but I can't go into an expert analysis of this text. I have very little time and a lot to get through. So everything you read out, I read out a moment ago, the very same thing.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we are -- we don't agree over one point: You say that Croatia accepted those weapons going through Croatian territory, and I claim that that was not what happened, because you can't see that from the president's text. He is making conditions. He is setting conditions to a step that he might take. So if you have other information from which you're able to conclude that, that's another matter, that the arms were nevertheless let through and passed through.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, all I'm saying is that you discussed the issue, and you said yesterday that you knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said precisely that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to deny this text. Please. I couldn't have denied it. There might be some misunderstanding, then, over that issue, what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, apart from this case, in any other case did you mention the letting through or sending of weapons to the BH army apart from in this text?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. As far as the -- the text is concerned and the sessions are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any information that the Croatian state let through and sent weapons to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I'm a legalist. I stick to the law, and if something -- if there is an embargo enforced by the international community on something, then anything that is done apart from that is trafficking, illegal, and smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At this meeting you said not a word. You uttered not a word about that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why should I?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, all right. That's an answer too, why should you. I'll accept that, let's end there. I'm going to skip over a few now --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now for the Judges -- I'd like to make this clear to the Judges at this point. What was discussed here was the letting through or not letting through of weapons. You have no evidence that the weapons were allowed to pass through as illegal goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, let me remind you that you said you can deal with that with other witnesses. I'm not the only witness to address this question. So let's leave it at that. You don't have to know anything, neither do we have to clear everything with you. Now, the meeting of the 2nd of July, 1993, is one you'll remember, I'm sure; the one that discussed the newspaper articles and the conflict, as you called it, with the president. It's the meeting where the president read out the letter from the British Prime Minister. You'll remember that, I'm sure. Now, I have your contribution to the discussion, and in what you said, you say that you're not going to give up on your position at all. You're not going to waiver from that, but you deny that anybody came to ask for Susak's replacement at that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we're once again dealing with specific individuals and specific requests, and I think that in this case it was an information trick, a ruse, where they said that I, General Tus, and some other people went to see the president, requesting that Mr. Susak be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you said you didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't do that and we denied that, but that foul play sort of was still bandied about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, on the Croatian translation, 01866481, you specifically said that you didn't ask anybody to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but I did this somewhere else. In a public interview, I asked -- I said that Susak should go.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, as a man of the law, as a legalist, can you explain to me how you asked that he should go in an interview whereas you say you failed to request this at a forum that discussed this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's my own up to me when I decide to say something, whether I'm going to say that I disagree with something at a session or whether I'm going to inform the public in another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you consider all that to be legal?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's all legal, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you don't raise problems where those problems are being discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep saying I should have done it at the session. I maintain that I should not have done it at the session. Why would I have to do it at that session? That's up to me. I can decide and choose.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All I'm asking is whether that's legal.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is legal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. We've finished with that now, let's move on to another area. And I'd like to note, having looked at all the transcripts we've had, I've looked through them all, and this brings me to the last transcript or the last session provided by the Prosecutor. The 4th of March, 1994, is the date. That's the time I'm addressing. It's 8012, the Prosecution Exhibit number, and you did not have anything -- you did not oppose anything at this meeting. You did not oppose the matters discussed. You made a few proposals but there was no confrontation on your part, either with Mr. Tudjman or Mr. Susak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how you came by that conclusion. I would have to ask you to read through all the transcripts now, and then you can see that I did stand up to those demands. I think that I did so in that particular transcript as well, that there was a direct conflict and clash between myself and the president on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What issue?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this transcript, if you want to see it, the one I mentioned, it is the 4th of March -- is that the one we're talking, about 4th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It speaks about a preliminary agreement on the creation of a Croatian-Muslim Federation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's an important event, an important matter, and you have my presentation there, which was quite lengthy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to leave it to the Judges to read through that transcript. Unfortunately, I haven't got enough time, but I'll say how you started off. "I think that the agreement was an ideal one from the standpoints of Croatia's interests. In the first place, the interests of the Croatian state because it will rid us and has rid us already, or freed us already, and I think that the example given by Gojko shows this, that had there not been an agreement, we would still have been under a blockade." So does all, everything you said glorify the agreement? Throughout that transcript there is not a single word you said during that transcript which would lead us to conclude that you had a conflict or clash either with Mr. Tudjman, the president, or with Mr. Susak either. But as I say, let's move on to another topic. I'm sure that everybody will read the transcripts carefully, and then we'll be able to see which of the two of us is right. Now, I'd like to go on, with the time that I have left before the break, to discuss a topic that I consider very important, and that's your book. Mr. Manolic, what was the object of your writing the book? Can you tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean; for the public or personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm talking about your book, and we have provided the interpreters with the book. All three booths have it. We're going to deal with the book, not too much, but it was printed, as I can see, in 1995. And is it, in a way, a sort of political promotion for your own party or a political invitation? Is that what you wanted to achieve with the book? Was that the meaning and purpose of publishing the book?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Had that been my aim -- the aim of publishing the book was in fact to see the difference between two policies waged towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the first point. And secondly, to highlight some of the problems in Croatian politics which clashed. So that was the object of that. Because in 1995, I don't know whether we had had the elections already then, whether there were any elections in 1995, but anyway, I wanted to round off the creation of the community and concluding with 1995, when I considered that the Washington Agreement had solved the problem as far as the way in which the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be solved.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. May we have a look at page 14 of your book together now, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just differentiate between your comments and what I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We'll do that, very quickly. If we take a look at page 14 of the book. I'm going to read it out, you'll have the text and you can follow so that you can see that I'm not interpreting. It is the -- they are the final two sentences on that page. You have the book in front of you. It is Prosecution Exhibit -- I apologise for not stating that beforehand because I see it's not up on our screens yet. Can somebody be of assistance? What Prosecution is it, the book, please? Some help, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me help you out. May I help you out and tell you that this is a comment, not my own presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Right. It is P 09673, exhibit, and page 14 of that exhibit. Yes, I'm saying it's your comment. I said that too. Did you take part in those comments?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You didn't take part at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commentator, the presenter may -- worked on the basis of political action thus far, on the basis of the interviews he had in front of him. That's what the editor did, and they're contained in the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But do you agree with his evaluations?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not with his evaluations, but as I see, each of these interviews where I speak directly are ones that I authorised.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we then say that it was the editor who said this, not you, "At the parliamentary elections, to give the vote to him and his party, the Croatian Independent Democrats would mean to vote for the humane, decent Croatian option which stands in defence of Croatian national interests and internationally recognised RH borders." So the editor says that. You have nothing to do with that; can we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you agree with what I say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we must not reject either my aspirations and efforts to introduce myself to the public as a political figure who advocated a certain course and policy. Whether that would be used in one set of elections or another set of elections was a minor problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I want to talk about, which course you advocated and when, in what period of time. Now, if we go to page 263 of the book, that would be your first interview given after the time that you said that you did not agree with the policies pursued by Croatia. It was on the 10th of September, 1993, that the interview was granted to the journal Globus. No. Just a minute I gave you the wrong page. The correct page is 256. The interview begins on page 256. Yes, on our screens, please, 256. That's an interview that you gave on the 10th of September, 1993. That's important. And I'm sure you remember the interview. You have the book to help you out. You recognise that certain differences of view exist in the HDZ, but as the reason you quote the following, and that is part of the text on page 257. The middle of 257, you say: "When we address practical matters, the implementation of HDZ policy, we can see that there are serious difficulties, that it is difficult to reconcile with respect to not advocating the functioning of a legal state against violence, against smuggling, and a respect for constitutionality and the laws." So we still don't see that you address your disagreement, your official disagreement with Mr. Tudjman as far as policy was concerned, or anybody else. You don't say that you don't agree with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who would this be against, then, targeted against? If I say as a prominent politician, if I am criticising the policies waged which are not geared to prevent crimes and offences from taking place, then it was somebody who prevented that from happening, which means against the person that waged the top-most state policy.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You and I know that presidents of republics, of states, don't arrest criminals. So let's stick to the text. In the text it says that you are disputing these matters with Croatian policy. All I'm saying is there's no mention of Bosnia there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In that same interview you speak about camps, and that is on page 262 of your book. This is the third paragraph from the top, and it begins thus: "This is one of the most difficult issues in the war. The camps, unfortunately, are a consequence of war. I personally condemn them. I condemn inhumane acts towards prisoners. Croatian politicians and statesmen loudly condemn the existence of camps, as did the opposition and clergy. However, all of this needs to be viewed in the context of war events. The Croats found themselves in a terrible mental shock. Their allies had become their enemies." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And at this moment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still adhere to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You still adhere to that. All right. Can we then turn to something else that might be quite interesting, which is your interview given on the 21st of January, 1994. This is the interview given to Globus.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think that the editor prepared the book in such a way so that it's quite confusing for an average reader, because they didn't bring your interviews in their entirety, they just brought certain sections of your interviews. I'm now going to focus on page 266. The bottom portion. The last paragraph, please. This is the part where you say that Mr. Boban urged the Croats from Bosnia to move out. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it's stated here. I don't know what's unclear about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's unclear when he sent this appeal to them. That's unclear to me. When was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had occasion to reply to me, because this was publicly announced. So he had every opportunity to reply to me whether this was true or not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I'm not here to defend Mr. Boban. Can you tell me specifically, if you remember, when is it you said this on the radio several times? So when did Mr. Boban do this? Give us the time frame. You say you spoke of this for the first time on the 21st of January, 1994. I'm asking you, very briefly, when did Boban send this appeal to them? When was it; in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely in 1994. It's quite possible in 1994, but I can't give you a firm date nor do I have these appeals, these calls, and his appearances on the radio and so on, but that can be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did I misunderstand you when you said during your first day of evidence that Boban sent this appeal to people to move out following the Graz Agreement between Boban and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know when this agreement was reached?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this was in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. And then in 1994 you bring this up again. Don't you think that an average reader, at least those who are familiar with events, can conclude that you sat on a piece of information for two years?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. It's not that I sat on a piece of information, but a policy and viewpoints are built over a number of years, not in one day, and this is what I mentioned in this particular interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I fail to understand. Mr. Manolic, this has nothing to do with policies or policy.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it have to do with, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are trying to make it appear that you were a defender of the sovereignty of the AVNOJ borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that you were consistent on that line of thoughts throughout the period. So I'm asking you, as a man who is putting up that image, how is it possible that you who participated in the highest level bodies of Croatia announced a piece of information two years later, whereas it was your duty and your obligation, Mr. Manolic, to request that Croatia take a firm position on that. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are not right. Just because this was my personal judgement as to when I was going to announce a particular argument and what I was going to present publicly. I was absolutely free in that sense, in political terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that you abused that freedom because you went along with Mr. Tudjman all the way up until there was a schism in your relations and then it was only then when that conflict broke out that you remembered all the things that should have been done while you were a member and an official in various official bodies.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that you are correct. Let us analyse all of my public statements given in -- given in public and at various sessions, and you will see that I didn't bring this up only in 1994, no. I brought it up much earlier. I firmly stood up against the policy which wanted to change the AVNOJ borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the Bench has the translation of this book. I hope that they will have it if this is introduced into evidence. But if it doesn't, and we would cover all interviews if I had sufficient time, it is my position that up until early hour there are absolutely no specific examples other than certain hints, other than certain hints --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: What you have actually -- you first proposed when you began your questioning, that you should slow down a bit, and also I would like to ask the witness, Mr. Manolic, also not to interrupt Ms. Nozica but to wait until the translation is being finished. I thank both of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, especially to you, but you are aware of the technical difficulties when we have, especially when communicating in the same language. Occasionally it is very difficult to stop this witness. This witness spoke about the Graz agreement and this agreement is becoming a bit of a legend here. Every witness seems to mention it, and every witness seems to draw conclusions on the basis of that agreement, and none of the witnesses who appeared here so far saw that agreement. Since Mr. Manolic spoke quite a lot about this agreement, he said that this was a key moment when two sides agreed on doing something, I would like for us thus to see Exhibit 2D 00040. 00192 is the exhibit number, page 0012. I apologise. Maybe I didn't give the right number. No, no, no, it is correct. Can we please see the document. Can it be pulled up on our screens. Yes. We can move on. Next page, please. Next page. That's it. Can we see it in Croatian, please. Next page, please. Next one, please. Now zoom in, please. I'm going to be reading this. Yes, precisely that's the portion I need. I want the interpreters to see this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is the text of the agreement, the agreement that you mentioned concerning which you said that you hadn't seen it. I'm going to put my question to you at the end. It says here: "Given that it is our intention to resolve all outstanding questions through agreement and in a peaceful way, including the border between our two constituent elements, Croatian and Serbian units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, representatives of Croatian and Serbian national communities have decided that in relation to the working demarcation map, there are the following specific differences: "1. In the town of Mostar, the Serbian side believes that the Neretva river is the border whereas the Croatian side believes that the entire town of Mostar is within the Croatian component unit." Can you, based on this, conclude that they agreed on anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they agreed on what is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that in Mostar the Serbian side believed that the Neretva was the border, whereas the Croatian side believed that the entire town of Mostar was within the Croatian unit. So this is just a statement on the state of agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude logically, linguistically, that they are dealing now with two interests, two opposing interests in item 1?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely. It can be seen here that they have agreed that they disagreed, and that means that they needed to continue their negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So no agreement. Item 2: "South of Mostar the Croatian side believes that the entire area which was drawn in 1939, that is to say the borders of Banovina, is within the Croatian unit. "The Serbian side believes that the border lies along the Neretva River. The border between the Croatian and Serbian units."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again this is a statement. They state that they failed to agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. 3: "Both sides agree that when delineating borders between these two units in the area of Kupres, Bosnian Posavina, Derventa, Bosanski Brod, Bosanski Samac, Odzak, Orasje, Modrica, and Brcko, they must take into account the compact nature of the terrain and the roads." Did they agree on anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On what, that they would take into account the compact nature of the terrain and the roads?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they also deviated from the ethnic principle. You can see here that Boban lost it here when it came to his principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't use that term, I'm a lady, after all. So if -- what you're saying is that this was to the detriment of Boban.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the detriment of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on to page 5. "Both sides are resolute that --"

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the text?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm looking at my text. "Both sides are resolute --" Can we please see the previous page, the previous page. The witness needs to see the previous page. I'm reading item 4. Yes. "Both sides are resolved to comply with the principles adopted at the Conference of European Community on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Pursuant to that, they have agreed that -- with the arbitration proceedings of European Community, they will adhere to the agreed criteria on defining national territory, both when it comes to problematic as well as to all other areas." I have no time to read the whole to text to you, but would you call this an agreement? You say that this is the first time that you see before you. Would you say that this agreement came up with any definite solution between these two units?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it defines the differences, the differences they had in their viewpoints, but it also accepted the arbitration, which was very important for the agreement itself, which means that they decided that in -- on issues where they disagreed, the arbitration would decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Whose arbitration?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say so here, but most likely some arbitration tribunal of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, it says here that they would abide by the principle adopted at the conference organised by the European Community about Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This was in 1991 or in 1992. Mr. Manolic, were they still dealing with the internal structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina? The structure was being discussed by various ethnic communities in the presence of the international community.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is it in your eyes illegitimate to discuss it in this way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not illegitimate at all. I think that every discussion, every meeting is a positive step, but the consequences of such discussions are another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, July -- Yes, correct, May.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Both you and I know that this was the period of time when Croats and Muslims in Bosnia fought together against Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you should also draw a conclusion that this agreement meant the end of this war between Croats and Muslims on one side and Serbs on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's not the conclusion that I can reach based on this.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But I can also conclude what you have concluded, namely that this is not an agreement. You took part in similar discussions, similar negotiations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that nevertheless this was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that's your position. And this is the main difference between some of the viewpoints of yours that you presented here and evidence that was adduced here. I have a suggestion here to put this question to you, and I'll do it gladly: Do you know who or, rather, who on the Serbian side liberated Mostar? Do you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now referring to 1992. Who liberated Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean liberated from Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was the Croatian units.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Croatian units?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not entirely sure. Don't hold me to this, but this was a detail which in operation -- operative matters could have been viewed in different ways. It's a matter for top politicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you said that this was the agreement that meant the final end to the conflicts with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that this agreement meant the end of conflict between Serbian forces and Croatian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina, mind you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel -- Counsel Nozica, I've been told that you've already used 90 [as interpreted] minutes. The division of time means that you have -- should have had 56 minutes. So would you please end quickly to give enough time for the other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that warning. I just want to say that the rest of the Defence counsel have told me how they're going to use their time, and I told them that I would be cross-examining until the first break. So I'm not taking anybody else's time. Yes, the time mentioned was 70 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think that we stopped with the forces that liberated Mostar. Which forces did you say? It says HVO, but which forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO. But in this case it was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So if the transcript says HV, it should read HVO. We'll put that right. And now our final topic. I'd like to say something with respect to your interview in Globus on the 22nd of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 317. Yes. On that page, for the first time or, rather, you did that before that on the 26th of March, 1994, in Novi List, that paper, just so you see that we haven't skipped that over, but anyway, on the 26th of April, 1994, in Novi List, at a point in time when your replacement is called for, you nominate -- you say that President Tudjman was the reason you did not agree.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because on the 22nd I had already been replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When I say the 26th of March you said this publicly, and I'll remind you of that. You have the book before you. It is page 285.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 6th of March, 1994. 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. You name President Tudjman for the first time there as being the person responsible. As the person who does not see eye-to-eye with you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the first time. That's my first point. And second point, I name him personally because when he spoke before the club of deputies, he stressed that he was taking over complete responsibility for the policy waged towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was my reaction to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was that Deputies Club held? Was it in October?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was all in March, the end of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So after that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after that. In the crisis that ensued in parliament, President Tudjman found it necessary to address the deputies because there was me and other Lower House representatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's when he asked for your replacement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a day here or there, but certainly the reason why I was to be replaced was addressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So was that during your -- the time you left. But anyway, I'd like to go to page 317, and that's the last thing I want to ask you about. It was an interview in Globus on the 22nd of April, 1994, and that is Exhibit -- we've already had the exhibit. It is the book. The page is 317, for everybody to be able to follow in the courtroom. You address Karadjordjevo. Page 317 of your book. The lower section of that page. The Exhibit number is P 09673, page 317. It says here that: "The president never, not even to his closest associates, said openly -" I hope the translators have the text - "of what he agreed with Slobodan Milosevic except for intimating some of the talks that were held. He said we couldn't tolerate that. During Tudjman's first negotiations with Milosevic the first cracks appeared in the policy of the Croatian Democratic Community." And then at the end, you say that Tudjman and Milosevic had agreed upon the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the toppling of the then Yugoslav Prime Minister Ante Markovic. In that same book of yours, which I have read very carefully, you have an introductory address to the parliament on the 16th of April, 1991, where you are in fact defending yourself from the attacks about the arrangement to replace Prime Minister Markovic. You say that that was never agreed upon. Here in court you said that Mr. Tudjman himself told you personally, and Mr. Mesic, that he was in Karadjordjevo and that they reached an agreement of principle about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you don't say that even in 1994 in these articles. You don't say that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't look for what I did not say, stick to the text and what I did say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says, "The president never told even his closest associates openly what he discussed with Slobodan Milosevic and the agreements they reached."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It said only in intimating what they discussed. Well, didn't that refer to the agreement on Bosnia and doesn't it emerge that he did not tell you that he had agreed upon what was to happen to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he told us in principle was a discussion on Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, in 1994, President Tudjman was still alive when this book came out.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you said for the first time that they had reached an agreement on Bosnia's division after President Tudjman's death.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, where did -- when did you say it while he was still alive?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm saying you didn't actually say it until the president died.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd having to go through the book, leaf through my book. I know that I did speak of that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wrote everything you -- I read everything you wrote in the book and you -- my conclusion is that you never ever said that while President Tudjman was still alive.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm trying to be quiet today but I don't understand the disagreement. On the very passage that counsel's referring to, it says at the end of that, "Tudjman and Milosevic agreed on division of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and counsel says that was never said before, but this book was published in 1995, at least five years before President Tudjman died. So I don't understand the dilemma. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just saying that for the record and for the Prosecutor. All I said was this: That the witness did not say, state in this interview that Tudjman had told him that they had reached an agreement. That's all I'm saying. Whereas here in court he said that Tudjman told him personally and Mesic, and speculations about Karadjordjevo were present before and after. So that's the only distinction I'm making, and I think it's quite clear now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want this to remain unexplained. President Tudjman, upon returning from Karadjordjevo, said, "We agreed in principle about the problems between Serbia and Croatia, which partially will go to the debit of Bosnia-Herzegovina." In principle. He didn't comment anything else, and we didn't ask him anything else. Our only comment was what about reality and reactions from third parties, or the third party, which meant the Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1991. Were there talks of that kind amongst all the parties?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't widespread.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But it was -- it did exist. Do you know the talks about SDA representatives with the Serb side before the referendum, the talks in Belgrade between Mr. Filipovic, Professor Filipovic? Do you know they talked in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that, that that was an agreement between part of the Muslims and the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was that about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something was known about that but it was negligible at the time, not important, because people like Filipovic and others weren't important figures. They didn't have an important political position.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know that Professor Filipovic went there with acquiescence from Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, then let's not conclude about things we don't know about. And finally, all I can do is repeat the question that I asked at the beginning: Your disagreements with the policy you expressed through the media, in the way in which we have seen, and you expressed them at the sessions that took place. And just three more minutes, with the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in direct contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
