utterances.text: Yes, direct contacts from the point in time when the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in 1991, at the first agreement in Karadjordjevo, and that is the period when the Serb aggression was fairly strong already vis-a-vis Croatia. And that is why this was not talked about broadly in public, the problem between -- and the issue of President Tudjman's meeting with Milosevic wasn't discussed widely at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know what Republika Srpska is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Manolic? Does it have all the attributes of a state within a state in the way in which you explained yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are we talking about? Are we talking about 1991 or after the Washington Agreements, or after the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before Washington and during the time that the Republic of Herceg-Bosna was established and after the Washington Agreements and after the Dayton Accords and to this day too. Did it have all the attributes of a state within a state? Did it have its constitution? Did it have its powers and authorities? Did it have its flag, and does it have that today? And is it today within the composition of that state, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is within the composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As it stands with its constitution, its flag, and all the attributes of statehood?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you when that came into being, as of what date, because at the beginning there was a lot of commotion going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was it recognised by the international community?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Washington and Dayton Accords, the international community did recognise it, yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was my final question. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just have one minute to indicate, as you mentioned yesterday, I do indeed request to have some time for redirect, so I will appreciate if that will be accounted for in the schedule. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I'd just like to note for the record that I am opposed to the admittance into evidence of the record and transcript because the witness said he wasn't sure he was there. I've just lost the number. The number -- just a moment, please. 1325. It is Prosecutor Exhibit 01325. I'm opposed to that because the witness did not confirm that he actually attended the meeting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. It is now 10.35. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, my name is Vesna Alaburic, attorney from Zagreb, and I'm here as Defence counsel for Milivoj Petkovic. Over the past seven years -- 17 years, I have always attended with great pleasure and satisfaction your public statements, and I'm going to ask you about your political fate after you left the HDZ and some topics that I consider to be relevant for this case. Just briefly, on the basis of Globus documents in which you published a series of interviews, Davor Butkovic and a series of other journalists always followed each of your reactions to the political events that were taking place. Now, if you have negative answers to my questions or you can't remember something, I am ready to show you the interviews, but if we manage to reach an agreement, we won't waste time on presenting the interviews. You have explained to us so far that on the 20th of April, 1993 -- 1994, I beg your pardon, in 1994, you were expelled from the HDZ, and you said that on the 25th of April of that same year, 1994, you formed a new political party of the Croatian Independent Democrats. Now, from those statements of yours one could conclude that when the new political party was -- that you worked to form a political party when you were still officially a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct organisationally speaking, but in the political sense certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Globus magazine of the 4th of -- 1st of April, 1994, which is highlighted in your book in part, you in fact put forward your political plans, made them public, which, if I'm allowed to summarise your words, boils down to the following: With Mr. Stipe Mesic you were to establish a new political party.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you expected that many HDZ members who were like-minded people would join that new political party. That's what you expected, and you thought that this would lead to a parliamentary crisis. You expected that thereby you would provoke a new set of parliamentary elections, and you had the support of the international public and the international community. You also enjoyed great support from the opposition and let me say the liberal public, if I can use that term. I hope we all understand what we mean when we saw that. And you were very realistic in considering that you could win power and authority in cooperation with the opposition at that year -- in that year 1994. Would that basically be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the object of every political party, to seize power, to come into power.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right. The elections were parliamentary. The parliamentary elections were held in Croatia in 1995, and your party at those elections was defeated.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, looking at Croatia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. And judging by your public statements you were disillusioned with the opposition in one way or another, and in 1996 you grew closer to Franjo Tudjman again and the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's correct in one aspect, that is to say that the question of relations with Serbia hadn't been settled yet. Relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been defined ultimately, and as a protagonist of those relations and as a person helping to solve those relations, I thought that I shouldn't come to loggerheads with President Tudjman but, rather, that on things we agree upon we could continue to cooperate. And the Washington Agreement found this common point. You can see that through my reactions and President Tudjman's reactions in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Washington was in 1994. We're now dealing with 1996 when you grew closer to the HDZ again. Let me mention Globus of the 12th of April, 1996, in which the editor-in-chief, Tonkovic at the time, and Davor Butkovic, the journalist, writes about the negotiations between you and Mr. Mesic with Tudjman, with President Tudjman, about cooperation. Several months later, on the 12th of July, 1996, the same author writes about the fact that the president of the country, Franjo Tudjman, and you were negotiating about the reconstruction of the government. Do you remember those newspaper articles? Do you want me to show them to you or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, at that period in 1997, round about, you made a number of favourable statements publicly about Franjo Tudjman, evaluating his statehood qualities and moves thus far. And so on the 14th of February, 1997, Globus published an article in which it was stated that your former party colleague, Stipe Mesic, who had in the meantime joined up with a third political party, criticised you for this open attachment to President Tudjman and the HDZ, and your position at the time was that the Republic of Croatia could only be led by the HDZ. That was your position at the time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of November, 1997, in a long interview once again in the Globus magazine, and I'm going to read out a portion of that interview because it's not included in your book, in response to a question --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to the Court. This will be an exhibit, so may we have it on e-court, and the number is 4D 00066. In the Croatian part of the text, that is to be found on page 2, it is underlined, highlighted, and I'm going to read out that part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I am reading your own words.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that portion included in the book?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. Your words are as follows: "Tudjman is a very successful and deserving politician. Let us be realistic. When over the past -- in 20 years history textbooks are written, they will naturally include the fact that Dr. Franjo Tudjman was the first president of independent -- on an independent Croatia and that it was under his leadership that Croatia won the war and retained all its state territory and strengthened its international status. The Herceg-Bosna project will be spoken of just as one of the less important deviations in the dramatic events in these regions." Just a small pause there. It's difficult for me to read out the following text. "That is the logic of history and the logic of politics, and we must all be conscious of that." Do you remember those words of yours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that, among other things, in the Jaratarnji List paper of the 28th of June, 1998, you said the following in a very -- rather long interview: "Croatia's future can only be resolved with Tudjman now." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unlike the praise you directed at the former Croatian president, Franjo Tudjman, the Prosecutor of this Tribunal has a dramatically different view of him. They consider him to be a criminal, as somebody who founded a criminal group which perpetrated many organised -- many acts of organised crime. Since you are somebody who cooperated closely with the former Croatian president and since you were his friend, would you please tell us whether he devised a criminal plan in a political or a military plan against Bosnian Muslims or other people? Do you have any such information about the former, the late Croatian president devising such criminal plans?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if creating a state within a state is considered a criminal plan --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Please tell us if he devised such plans.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "plans"?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know of him devising some plans - I was quite specific - of political and military acts against Bosnian Muslims? Did you ever hear of Franjo Tudjman devising such plans?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All his plans can be reduced to his entire political influence, which is evidenced by these transcripts in its entirety, through all of these transcripts taken together. This is a good reflection of his policies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for your answer to be recorded. Mr. Manolic, the transcripts that we have today during these sessions, were they recorded without the knowledge of President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given your experience, both in police work and intelligence services and in politics, given that you're a lawyer, did you ever come across a situation where a president of a state is devising criminal plans during the sessions, is publicly recording these sessions, transcribing them, or do you think that that would be an unprecedented event in history?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered a similar question yesterday; namely, that President Tudjman, with his public appearances, or, rather, in all of his public speeches, in all the sessions and so on, never referred directly about him being in support of the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So can we conclude that you never attended a meeting nor did you ever read anything about Franjo Tudjman devising any criminal plans?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. We'll get to that. Now you are telling us about a state within a state. You said to Ms. Nozica that your disagreement with Croatian policy vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina was expressed following the creation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, which was in August of 1993. Therefore, I will remind you of the interview you gave to the Danas magazine on the 12th of October, 1993. I will refer you to the portions which omitted in your book. I will now give your words in full, and I will attach this when objecting to this book being tendered into evidence, because it doesn't contain all of the interviews in their full form. You said the following: "So far I don't know of any agreement between Milosevic and Tudjman." And then you proceeded to say: "Would that mean the abolishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in its present form?" Or, rather, that was the question. And then you answered to that: "Would that be an abolishment or not, what is important for us is that national interests are respected, national interests of all ethnic communities residing within the territory of the state." Then you give a reply, which is included in the book, but you omitted the last sentence, and the last sentence reads: When speaking of internal units within Bosnia and Herzegovina, you said as follows: "Is this going to be in the form of a republic or some other kind of autonomy is something that needs to be agreed upon, is something that should be resolved through agreement." Based on this, we can conclude that in October of 1993 you knew of the existence of a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. You believed that it was completely irrelevant whether it was going to be a republic or another form of autonomy, which is contrary to what you said to us today.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is contrary. I don't think there is anything contrary there. In the first portion you read out, and it needs to be clear to everybody, you read out first the question of the journalist, and the question is different from my reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. I stated quite clearly what is the question and what is an answer.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't. It wasn't clear even to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question was: "Would that mean an abolishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in its current form?" That was the question. And to this you answered with another question: "Whether that's going to be an abolishment or not, what is important for us is that national interests be respected." So for you it was irrelevant whether there was going to be abolishment or not.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to say, that the process of looking for solution in Bosnia-Herzegovina was ongoing. That was the essence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I would like to remind you of an interview published in Globus on the 18th of June, 1993, which can also be found in your book, but without the portion that I'm going to quote now. When asked whether the policy in Bosnia is the main point of disagreement, in June of 1993 you said as follows: "I don't think that that's the main reason. The main reason are our internal problems."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you need to depict the entire context.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The interviews need to be in their integral -- in their entirety. I agree with you. Now let us go back to our late president, Franjo Tudjman. You said to us today that he was a realistic politician.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that Franjo Tudjman took great -- or, rather, devoted a lot of attention to the reactions of various international institutions, to the reaction of the international community as a whole when it came to Croatian policies within the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this is clear from all of the transcripts that that was his attitude towards the international community. He believed that the decisions of the international community had to be complied with because that had a great impact on the further development of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the point in time when the international community took the position that the former Yugoslavia could fall apart, could go through a process of disassociation but that the former republics had to remain within their AVNOJ borders, would you say that that position was a firm axiom that Franjo Tudjman respected, that he believed that that position needs to be complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you say that Franjo Tudjman was the first one who supported the international arbitration about the former Yugoslavia and the involvement of the international community in the resolution of the Yugoslav problem?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was Franjo Tudjman among the first one who supported the idea of the UN peacekeeping forces coming to the territory of the former Yugoslavia, among other things, in order to assure peace?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the decision of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But was that also the initiative that was launched in our area? Was it our politicians who launched this solution?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you have to be aware of the circumstances existing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm very well aware of them. Would you agree with me that Franjo Tudjman was a person who wanted the peacekeeping forces to be deployed to the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina? You spoke of this in your interviews.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Knowing Mr. Tudjman both as a politician and as an historian, tell us, would he have ever consented to creating and building a Croatian state on the basis of something that could be considered a crime, or do you think that, given the historical perspective, he would have believed this to be impermissible?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you need to be specific about the context based on which you draw such conclusions. If the issue of the change of borders is analysed, then we have to say that President Tudjman accepted the Badinter Commission and its decisions that the borders so far have been transformed into state borders. However, his talks with Milosevic disrupt that, go against this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Manolic, I have already taken up some time of my colleagues, so let us see if we proceed quickly. Now let us deal with Karadjordjevo and this infamous conversation between Tudjman and Milosevic on the 25th of March, 1991. In the three and a half days of your testimony so far, you gave us some very contradictory evidence about this, as you did in your public statements.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your view.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll explain my view. I'm sure that you will help us clarify this, namely that they discussed the division within Bosnia and Herzegovina, the internal division. You said today to Ms. Nozica that in that meeting, as Franjo Tudjman told you, Tudjman and Milosevic agreed on problems between Croatia and Serbia which was partially going to be to the detriment of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that not a single word was uttered about the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what does it mean "to the detriment of Bosnia and Herzegovina"? What do you understand in that -- that that term means?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, on pages 54 and 57 of transcript, you said that Franjo Tudjman and Slobodan Milosevic agreed in principle on division of Bosnia. On the same day, on pages 77 to 79 of the transcript, you said that the two of them reached an agreement on the division within Bosnia and Herzegovina, inside Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you mentioned the word "inside" or "within" at least three times. And then you added that, unlike them, Alija Izetbegovic supported the idea of integral Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this statement of yours was recorded on page 80 of the transcript on the 3rd of July. On the same day, on pages 94 and 97, and also on the 5th of July, on pages 163 -- on page 163, you said to us as follows: That desires are one thing and reality is something quite different, that Franjo Tudjman did not want any changes of borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina because that would not have been accepted by the international community.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed that today. And then just another addition about what you said to -- about Karadjordjevo. On the 5th of July, which was recorded on page 25 of the transcript, when discussing that meeting in Karadjordjevo, you said: "No. I didn't say that they had reached an agreement on division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, rather that they were discussing it. I don't know to what extent this nuance can be conveyed through translation, but to reach an agreement is a finite verb, whereas to discuss or to negotiate is something that implies that no agreement has yet been reached. It's a continuing process." So I will ask you this now: In November of 1991, they were discussing the future of the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the then Yugoslavia. The presidents of six republics would meet regularly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the sessions of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In March of 1991, the political options were as follows: Serbia and Montenegro supported the concept of the federation. Slovenia and Croatia supported the confederation concept, and they proposed a certain transition period, to last between five and ten years during which internal division would be completed and all contentious issues resolved. In June of 1991, a certain compromise was -- compromise solution was presented by the presidents of Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Gligorov and Mr. Izetbegovic, who proposed an asymmetrical federation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something similar to confederation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. What they called an asymmetric federation, partially a confederation, partially a federation.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which was a modified proposal of Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Correct. Would you agree with me that in March of 1991, when the meeting in Karadjordjevo was held, the creation of independent states from the republics of the former Yugoslavia was not an option, especially not an option that Milosevic was ready to reach an agreement on with somebody.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that was a fait accompli, because even before these conversations in 1991, there was already a rebellion of Serbs in Croatia, in 1990 and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We will get to the subject of these discussions, but completely independent of that, I'm asking you now about the political options. What else was discussed in the state at the time? Let me repeat my question: I hope you will agree with me. In March of 1991, they discussed the future of Yugoslavia, and the creation of independent states from the former republics of Yugoslavia was not an option on the table.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in principle it wasn't; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the logical conclusion would be that in that same month, March of 1991, they also discussed the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite naturally. Would you agree with me that all of us - almost all of us - considered Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a mini Yugoslavia? Was that the general thesis?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the general one, no. That was the position taken by some politicians but not a general position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was the concept that was supported back in the socialist times, in colloquial terms, due to the fact that the population was so mixed we believed Bosnia-Herzegovina to be a good example of mini Yugoslavia. So would you say that if any changes of internal structure of Yugoslavia were discussed, wouldn't you say that it was natural that they also discussed the future of this mini Yugoslavia, which is precisely why the topic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was very current at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was topical because of its composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serbs attacked. They wanted to join that part to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. We'll come to that. We'll come to who wanted what. But the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a question that was opened up, because of the composition or because it was Yugoslavia in miniature. Now, would you agree with me that already at that time talks had started about the internal set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that there were diametrically opposed views about that on the part of the individual ethnic groups or constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Everybody had his own view to protect their own national interests, each ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Now, would you agree with me if I put it to you -- well, the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina are not under dispute. We had the Badinter Commission, the conclusions were made. So we're not dealing with borders any more. Now, would you agree with me when I say that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina strove to have Bosnia-Herzegovina remain within Yugoslavia, and in case that did not happen, that they publicly let it be known that the territory which they had pretensions on would be organised as their own --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, state, province, region, whatever. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were in favour of having Bosnia and Herzegovina not remain within Yugoslavia and that they wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be organised as a complex state according to the national criterion, so that each of the three constituent peoples had a certain territory and region in which they would be the majority population?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that you, in all of your public statements, supported those positions of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they -- you considered them to be rational and justified?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, I would like -- at this point, Your Honour, these questions have to be more precise. When she talks about "supported those positions of the Croatian people," which positions, at which time, in what part of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is it Herceg-Bosna, is it some other group, is it the Posavina? This question is far too broad for this witness to answer in a meaningful way. Time, place, which agreement, what territory, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness understood what I asked him and he gave us an answer. Now, this question can only be unclear to somebody who does not have full knowledge, and I apologise to Mr. Scott, I don't wish to insult him, but for those of us coming from those regions we know exactly what we're talking about. So the question was very specific and we understood it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I did warn you of the time, the period we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking about Karadjordjevo, 1991, and we're developing our thoughts along those lines. We'll come to Herceg-Bosna, we'll come to the republic. I think somebody wanted to intervene behind me. No? Fine, then let's proceed. And we agreed about the positions of the Croats. Now all that remained was the Bosniaks or, rather, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I object again. I'm sorry, Mr. Manolic, please allow me to object. The position of the Croats. There were many different positions of the Croats. There were the Kljuic Croats, there's the Boban Croats, there's other Croats. You can't just ask a question about "all the Croats agreed." With all respect, it's not proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Manolic, when you are answering the question, in your mind are you thinking of the Croats in general or do you make distinctions between the different types of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think we have to distinguish between them, because it was one thing to look at the position of the main Croatian force in Bosnia, which was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us what distinctions you make. How do you distinguish between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I distinguish between them in the following way: One portion were for Bosnia-Herzegovina to continue, whereas others allowed for the possibility of seceding or, rather, stepping down from that community. That would be a better expression.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I'm not asking you now about an integral or not integral Bosnia-Herzegovina because I consider that we have solved that topic and dealt with it because we said that the borders cannot be changed. Therefore, we're talking about the internal system and set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask my question and things will become much clearer, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I do not agree that that issue has been resolved. I just want to make it very clear that we don't consider that, and if that's counsel's position, I want to make it very clear the Prosecution does not consider that to be resolved and does not consider that to be the full scope and character of Mr. Manolic's testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Judges will consider that matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The question remains for us to say which Croats we're talking about in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it take part in the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, if you have that information as a former head of the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia, how many or what percentage of the Croat population in Bosnia-Herzegovina voted in favour of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, I don't think you're being precise. If you're looking at the referendum and the question posed at the referendum --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, we'll come to the referendum in due course.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact percentage, but the vast majority, I think it was about 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the third largest ethnic group in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims, or the Bosniaks, would you agree with my following position about that: That for a long time they tried to find a compromise solution with respect to whether they were going to stay within Yugoslavia or step down from Yugoslavia, and at the end of 1991, after the international community had stipulated the conditions for the recognition of individual republics as independent states, decided to ask for recognition of their independence, that is to step down from Yugoslavia, and as far as their internal system was concerned, what they wanted was a unitary state which would function according to the principles of one man, one vote, a commonly known principle.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you. I'm not saying you said it. I'm asking you, what do you say no to of all that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that they were for a unitary state. I think that they came to represent the three constituent elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you told us in your testimony so far that the Muslims or, rather, Alija Izetbegovic, advocated a unitary state and that throughout that time in all the negotiations they in fact endeavoured to avoid any territorial delineation and separation and wanted to have an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that came to the fore in a certain period of time, but I think that ultimately that position was not upheld.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, that's right. It wasn't ultimately upheld.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at certain points in time that was the position taken by that group of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please, Mr. Manolic, in view of the fact that you made public statements with respect to the plans made by the international community about the former Yugoslavia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina included, I assume that you were well-versed in this matter. Tell us, please, who at those negotiations represented the Croatian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance? Was it Mr. Mate Boban, Mate Boban, was it Miro Lasic, or some other person from Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the character of the conference. I don't know which one you're referring to now. But in principle when we were having international conferences and when it was case of the positions in the Yugoslav state Presidency, which still existed at the time, then in that case it was always Izetbegovic who represented the community, with a Presidency member from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, if you know, who on behalf of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina signed the Vance-Owen Plan, for instance, in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the name of whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the name of the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could only have been Boban. Boban was the only person who could have signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who took part in the negotiations and then possibly signed certain documents in the name of the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Karadzic could have been the only man to have been able to do that. Or Koljevic perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And at those negotiations did somebody represent the Muslims, the Bosniaks? Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they did, then it must have been either the minister later on of foreign affairs, or it might have been Izetbegovic himself. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now from your answer, am I to conclude that at those negotiations and in those documents Mr. Alija Izetbegovic did not represent Bosnia-Herzegovina but, rather, he represented the Muslims or, rather, the Bosniaks within Bosnia-Herzegovina? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to differentiate between that now. At that period of time it was difficult to distinguish. He always represented the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, well that's not contentious. We're all in favour of an integral Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene at this point. The three Judges are looking at the clock. There are two more Defence counsel who wish to conduct their cross-examination, and of course the Prosecution would like to ask supplementary questions and so on. So time is our concern. How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, our agreement is as follows: Mr. Ibrisimovic has waived his right to take up time, and with the Defence counsel of Valentin Coric, my colleague, I decided that I would give ten minutes of time before the break so that she could continue after the break and then leave 15 or so minutes for the Prosecution's questions and another ten minutes for general matters. And I would also like to suggest that documents be tendered on Monday, because we're really under great time constraints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So that means that you would be finishing by 12.20; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So now to go back to my question, Mr. Manolic. If a document, Stoltenberg -- Stoltenberg's, Owen's, Vance-Owen's is signed by Karadzic, Izetbegovic and Boban, the question is who does Mr. Izetbegovic represent? Would you agree that he is signing in the name of the Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was still president.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's something else. That was his position. But who was he representing at those conferences?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international negotiators --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, wouldn't it be better to look at the documents themselves and see how they're signed? And if they're sign as President Izetbegovic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we know without speculation how they're signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Alaburic. You were referring to what document, what period, what date? Don't forget that Mr. Izetbegovic was the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, he was legally bound to sign all international documents. Mr. Praljak, if it's really important, go ahead, but otherwise you're taking up time. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Izetbegovic was never the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was president of the Presidency, and legally speaking, he had to take a Croat and a Serb to negotiations with him from the Presidency, if everything was to be legal. He was one of one of seven equal members. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it comes to the same thing, Praljak. It boils down to the same thing. He was president of a Presidency, a collective body, and collective bodies never attended fully in their -- in negotiations; you would have the president of the Presidency appearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with respect to Mr. Scott's comment and objection, I'd like to say the following: I did not intend to question Witness Manolic with respect to the formal contents of individual agreements and contracts signed by the representatives of three national communities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The agreements that I have to date are contained in this book, and they do not contain signatures. Now, I'm asking Mr. Manolic as an individual who made public statements, which is borne out by his book, about certain agreements and treaties signed as somebody who kept abreast of political events and took part in meetings with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and who knows full well that at those international conferences individuals represent -- there were people representing the three ethnic groups of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that nobody represented Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. There is no dilemma for me on that score, that Mr. Manolic is very well aware of that. So I haven't prepared documents with the different signatures, but we'll clarify that in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you must be specific. When we're talking about an agreement or a document, the Vance-Owen document, for instance, that the international representatives wanted to have a certainty and guarantees, not for just one man's signature, such as Izetbegovic's signature as president of the Presidency, but the signatures of the conflicting parties and warring parties in that territory, because only in that way could a solution be found. Because the conflict existed, there was a conflict, that's quite clear. Otherwise, there wouldn't have been any need for the representatives of those national groups, the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims to sign any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. They signed a document. The people who signed the document were those who were discussing something, three national groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina or ethnic groups discussing the internal set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am not questioning that the documents that Alija Izetbegovic signed with, for example, the president of the Croatian state, that Mr. Izetbegovic was signing as president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is not being contested, but I'm talking about something quite different now. I'm saying who is it who articulates the position of the Bosniak people at international conferences? Who is their porte-parole and who says what the Bosniaks want in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Silajdzic as the Muslim representative who also took part at those conferences, and that he articulated their desires and made requests, and he clashed with the other sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about anybody above him? Was he the number one man or was there anybody above him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that. You would have to look at their statute and their legal provisions who the number-one man was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was Silajdzic? What post did he hold and at what time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, as far as I remember, that he was one of the leaders of the Muslim community in Bosnia-Herzegovina who went from one position to another. At a point in time I think he was foreign minister --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was he Alija Izetbegovic's boss?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was Alija Izetbegovic his boss?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were their relationships. I don't want to enter into that now. But constitutional hierarchy states who was whose boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was the president of the SDA at that time, the Party of Democratic Action, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they rotated, that people changed. I couldn't tell you exactly now who it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I'm sure you remember that, I'm sure you can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were always under the influence of the number one figure and personage, who was Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But listen, Silajdzic didn't attend meetings very often. Was it then Izetbegovic who articulated the views of the Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which sessions you have in mind, but I remember that Silajdzic participated both in some international conferences as well as in contacts with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you don't remember Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about him.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm telling you. I told you that the main figure in that entire hierarchy of Bosniak Muslims in BH was Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So we agree. Mr. Manolic, I would now like to establish the extent of your knowledge as to whether the Croats of BH or, rather, the leadership of Herceg-Bosna accepted the plans of the international community or whether they obstructed these plans. Yesterday you gave us very extensive answers to the questions of Mr. Prlic's lawyer about Stoltenberg's plan. I know that in your interviews you publicly presented your views on certain plans of the international community, so with your permission I would like to cover with you briefly some of these plans to see what was the position of the leadership of Herceg-Bosna. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was hoping -- I was hoping not to be on my feet so much today. This witness has said since Monday that he was only in -- throughout this entire period he was only in Bosnia perhaps once, in Sarajevo in August, 1990. He has also said that he did not have operational dealings with any of these people. Herceg-Bosna, if you will, was not his beat. It was Mr. Susak's beat. It was his responsibility. So if -- with all respect, with the greatest of respect for Ms. Alaburic, if questions are going to be put to the witness about the specific positions of Mr. Prlic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Stojic, then at this point, Your Honour, I have to ask for a specific foundation as to his personal knowledge to be able to express a view on that, and that is inconsistent with everything he has told us for the last three and a half days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam, if you lay the foundations first, then he can discuss Mr. Prlic, Stojic, Praljak, and so on, but providing that he knows him and that he saw them before. If he has never seen them before, then we are embarking on speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Witness Manolic testified almost exclusively about the fact of existence or non-existence of joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution brought Mr. Manolic here so that he could confirm that there existed criminal plans of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina and Bosniak people, and also that the Republic of Croatia, via the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, implemented those plans. In that context, I believe it to be very important to ask how these Croats then treated the plans of the international community and the efforts of the international community to find a peaceful resolution to all problems. It is our position, and we have evidence that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the Croats of Croatia were extremely cooperative in their cooperation with the international community, jointly seeking solutions that would be acceptable to all three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they were the first and sometimes the only ones who signed all plans which certain representatives of the international community offered, and we believe this to be one of the elements going to prove that the joint criminal enterprise does not exist and that the allegations contained in those counts of indictment, 15, 16, and 17 are not true, and those are the ones referred to directly by the Prosecution. We believe this to be directly linked to the responsibility of all the accused in this trial. Now, as to the issue of individual guilt, we'll get to that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Manolic was brought here to address a particular scope of evidence, and that was -- the -- what was happening in Zagreb among the senior Croat leadership; Mr. Tudjman, Mr. Susak, Boban when he came to Zagreb. This man never met Boban once in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or with Prlic or with Stojic. And I agree that limits his testimony, but he wasn't offered for that reason. He met Mr. Prlic in one meeting in Zagreb. I'm talking about their dealings in Herceg-Bosna on the ground in dealing with these matters. This witness was brought to The Hague by the Prosecution to deal with the issue of the leadership -- senior leadership in Zagreb, and that's what he's talked about consistently. Secondly, as the second part of Ms. Alaburic's statement of her position, I understand that's their position. They can call witnesses. They can call evidence on that point. They can try to establish their position, but not through this witness who has no personal knowledge. I invite them to call their evidence, and it will be all subject to

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: through this witness who was not involved in any of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Scott, the Defence, via Ms. Alaburic, claims that you brought this witness here so that he could support the thesis of the Prosecution on joint criminal enterprise. I listened to you carefully. I checked the transcript, and it seems that you are saying that you didn't bring this witness for that purpose but, rather, so that he could explain what was going on in Zagreb and whom he saw in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain to me, then, what was your object in bringing this witness here? Because if you didn't bring him here to give evidence about joint criminal enterprise, then it's quite normal for the Prosecution -- for the Defence to cross-examine on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest respect, you misinterpret and misstate the Prosecution's position. Yes, of course it's our position. It wouldn't be in the indictment otherwise if we didn't charge a joint criminal enterprise having various facets and involving various people over various times at various levels. Part of that joint criminal enterprise - part of it - is what happened in Zagreb. That is what this witness came to talk about; what happened in Zagreb, how it was directed from Zagreb, what the transcripts show, the meetings that he was involved in, how it was directed from Zagreb by people like Susak and Tudjman and others. He was not brought -- and I think I know why I brought this witness to The Hague -- he was not brought to talk about meetings that he had with Stojic or Prlic or anyone in Grude or Mostar, or anyone else. There's no issue that he did not have. No one has suggested -- in three and a half days no one has suggested he had such meetings, and that's not the reason he's offered. Now, if Ms. Alaburic can establish personal knowledge, a foundation for this witness to express a view over what each of these individuals did during this time, then if she can establish that foundation, I have no objections. I will sit down and I -- and she can ask all the questions she wants if she establishes that this witness has personal knowledge to talk about those things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may very briefly, and I did seek leave from Ms. Alaburic. The gentleman has accused President Tudjman, Susak, Bobetko, all of the accused of being criminals. He stated -- excuse me, sir. Excuse me, sir. You can disrupt the Prosecution. I pointed to the record specifically where he pointed to the third echelon. That was very clear. That was very clear. So I think the questions that are being posed by Ms. Alaburic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, just a minute. We need to clarify something. We seem to remember, but we didn't discuss this among us, he never said at any point in time that Mr. Susak was a criminal. He said that there had been crimes, but he didn't accuse either Mr. Tudjman or Mr. Susak as criminals. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it is you who is creating that link.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... going to see in the final brief of the Prosecution is this gentleman's testimony, where he's saying that President Tudjman, along with Susak and others, were trafficking guns and trafficking all sorts of other material, sending troops over, financing troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina, all going into the joint criminal enterprise. That's what this gentleman has said. Now, I know he's got to go back to Croatia and face the people, and perhaps that's why now he's trying to be on both sides of the fence, but he can't claim on the one hand for the president of Croatia to be financing troops and sending troops into Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the Defence minister to be engaged in trafficking of weapons, to be engaged in those sorts of illegal activities with banks, and at the same time say, well, I'm not accusing them. I think that's what we're going to find from the Prosecution. That's their theory of the defence. And I think it's perfectly legitimate for Ms. Alaburic to go into these areas. Now he can't have it both ways; I don't know what's happening in Bosnia but at the same time, when I'm being questioned by the Prosecution, he testifies to this. Now today he was even telling us he doesn't know who Izetbegovic was representing. This is pure confabulation. And I think this is very relevant and I think Ms. Alaburic is at the point of establishing that the gentleman is not being truthful and honest with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all right. Ms. Alaburic. Let me specify that you still have about 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I assume I don't need to remind you that in your interviews to Vecernji List on the 29th of May, 1993, you spoke of Vance-Owen Plan, you commented on certain provisions from that plan. Based on that, I conclude -- and I know that you are one of the most responsible politicians in my country, so based on that I'm sure that you read what you commented on. I assume that you were also familiar with other plans of the international community. Prior to Vance-Owen Plan in January of 1993, there were a number of plans, such as Cutileiro Plan from March of 1992, there was a draft of the constitutional set-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina from October of 1992, which was drafted by the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia. There was also Owen-Stoltenberg Plan from July of 1993. We spoke of it yesterday. And then Washington Agreement, Dayton Accords, and so on. Are you familiar with all of these plans?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that wasn't the case, you wouldn't be putting that question to me, but I stated my position in that interview, in various public appearances, and it was recorded. So there is nothing disputed there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever. I hope we'll resolve this within a minute if you are going to agree to what I'm putting to you. In Cutileiro Plan in March of 1992, it was envisioned that Bosnia-Herzegovina would comprise several constituent units on the ethnic principle, and then a working plan was established to come up with a map. The representatives of Croats accepted that plan. Agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: In October of 1992, the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia came up with a constitutional set-up, a draft of it, based on which BH was supposed to have seven to ten autonomous provinces, most of which would have one of three ethnic groups as the majority one. Each province would have its own legislative, executive and judicial power, whereas the army would exist at the level of the central government. The representatives of the Croatian people in BH accepted this constitutional structure of BH. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: In January of 1993 Vance-Owen Plan --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to say, Who disagreed with the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get to that. I'm now focusing on the Croats first to see what was their attitude with respect to the international community's plan. All right. Vance-Owen plan in 1993, Bosnia-Herzegovina comprises ten autonomous provinces, each of them has its own legislative, executive and judicial branch. The Croats would be a majority in three out of ten provinces. Boban signed all of the documents in relation to Vance-Owen Plan in January of 1993. Agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to say, you have to specify who disagreed with the plan.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Karadzic disagreed with everything. Alija Izetbegovic signed a portion. He didn't sign the maps. Later on, he changed his mind. As Mr. Karnavas said, he would have one position in the morning and one position in the afternoon. Then we have Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, July, Bosnia-Herzegovina comprising three constituent republics. Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed to that plan immediately. In Geneva it was also accepted by Alija Izetbegovic, but on the following day, he withdrew his consent to the plan and asked for guarantees that the union of three constituent republics would have all attributes of a state. However, representatives of all three peoples, Boban, Karadzic, and Izetbegovic, continued negotiations on maps. Agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What am I supposed to confirm here or reject? This was published. These are the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes, the facts. Can we, based on this, conclude justifiably that the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not obstruct a single plan of the international community, a plan for peaceful resolution to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't phrase this question correctly. The Croats accepted this division into provinces because they were awarded three provinces which, in the national sense, satisfied the Croats because these three provinces covered the geographic area where Croats resided.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now have to wrap up our discussion here, Mr. Manolic, and there will be three questions which are not individually related to each other. Banovina Croatia. Yesterday, Mr. Kovacic gave you the constitution of the Republic of Croatia where the Banovina is mentioned in the preamble. Do you remember that, or do we need to put it before you on the ELMO? You remember the preamble?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there's nothing contentious there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: No, nothing whatsoever. I want something else. The constitution you had before you is not the constitution of 1990 but rather the constitution of 2001. So it was the revised text which was changed at the time when Stipe Mesic was in power, Ivica Racan, who was Prime Minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: So under their leadership the constitution also contained a provision on the Banovina of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not contained in Croatian constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: The constitution of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the preamble is quite a different matter. So the preamble was not amended. It remained the same. It was the Tudjman's preamble.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes. Quite correct. If Stipe Mesic and Ivica Racan left it in the constitution, would that mean a firm evidence that this was not an expression of territorial claims but, rather, this was an evidence of the continuity of Croatian statehood, as Mr. Kovacic said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct. That was the meaning of the preamble.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I will always remember you, and most of the Croatian public will remember as you as a person who spoke up quite a lot against the terrorism in the territory of Croatia. You spoke about looting, destruction of public property. You supported the rule of law. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite, but it has nothing do with what we're discussing here.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and I'll tell you why. Tell me this first, please, though: Would you agree with me if those same events, let us call them terrorist activities for the time being, took place on the territory of the Republic of Croatia during the war, even towards the Croatian population not only towards the Serbian population of the Croatian Republic, would you agree with me that then those same evil acts towards the Muslim and Bosniak population in Bosnia-Herzegovina would -- could be grouped into the same set of problems and come under the heading of terrorism on the part of criminal groups which in wartime are very difficult to keep under control? So would you agree that what was happening in Croatia and what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina were the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. It would be difficult to apply analogy there which would be able to cover everything as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Well, not as a whole, but basically.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Terrorism, crimes, that all comes under the same sort of chapter whether it's international or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll also remember you as an individual who spoke very reasonably about the involvement of professionals in the army and the police when you talked about the Serbs who were in the army the police on the territory of the so-called Krajina region and when you strove for the fact that their dismissal and involvement in the police and the military should be treated as their professional involvement and that should not be an impediment for their integration into the Croatian army and Croatian police force. Do you remember those statements of yours?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say now that I was president of the commission which President Tudjman appointed to resolve problems of relationships between the Serbs and Croats, and that is when I reached that conclusion that in order to resolve Serbo-Croat relations, that that can only be done if professionalism be accepted and if these people could be incorporated into the structures of the Croatian state, because otherwise it would have been impossible. And I think that I was quite clear on that score in explaining why.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes, you were quite clear, that's true. I apologise to the interpreters for talking so quickly. Yes, as I was saying, I think you were reasonable and that your comments were well founded and very welcome, but as the Defence counsel of a Croatian general at this point in time who was a professional officer whichever way you look at it, he was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army to begin with, I have to ask you whether those positions of yours hold true for professionals in the HVO, too, or do you consider that in the Croatian Defence Council there were officers and soldiers who professionally did their duty?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but we can only talk about specific cases, not in bulk.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Tell me, do you know General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By sight.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Right, by sight. Do you know that he was promoted when the social democratic liberal powers that be were established in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: That he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Now, tell me, do you know that the -- President Stipe Mesic, as his personal envoy, sent him to the Sinj Alka celebration. For those of you who don't know, it's a traditional event in a place in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that, whether he was sent, who sent him, whether he was an envoy or what. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION WHEN THEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Manolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I thank the Court and cede the floor to my colleague. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Before I begin the cross-examination, I would just like to tell Their Honours that my client and I have agreed to divide up our time in such a way as a brief portion of the time would be taken up by my cross-examination and I leave my client to do the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you representing then? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, I'm a lawyer from Zagreb, and I represent Mr. Valentin Coric in this case.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A client whom I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, without my having to ask you. So let's get going. Mr. Manolic, tell us, please, if I understood you correctly, you told my colleague Ms. Nozica today that you authorised all your interviews.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 99 per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Tell me now, please, when they -- when authorising your interviews you ever asked any portions to be reacted from them.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that probably happened. It was my relationship towards the journalist who conducted the interview, and that happens to everyone. It's quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I'd like to ask you this: Dunja Ujevic, does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you know Ms. Ujevic from?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She did an interview with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: May we have Exhibit 5D 00478, please. 5D 00478 is the number of the document, please. The name is Dunja Ujevic, for the transcript, for the record. The page is 84, line 14. Her name is Dunja Ujevic. Mr. Manolic, I'm going to read the text out to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a false text. Let me tell you that straight away. You're taking me back to World War II.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a false text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Manolic, you can say that it is a lie, but allow the Defence counsel to present her point of view and then you can say that it's all a lie. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: The text reads as follows: "The former column journalist writer Vecernji List Dunja Ujevic testified that Josip Manolic, at the time president of the Chamber of Counties in the Croatian Sabor parliament reacted when she asked him a question of the 200 civilians whom the partisans had killed without a trial in Bjelovar. "When in talking to Manolic I asked him that question, he lost his nerve and he looked at me for a long time and then he got up from the table and started shouting, "Guards, guards," stresses Dunja Ujevic. Then he calmed down suddenly. He got out a small black comb from his pocket and started coming his hair. After that, he said to my quite calmly they were not civilians, they were quislings. He described the atmosphere -- or, rather, the atmosphere was described in that way by the journalist of Vecernji List. After that, something happened that I had never experienced either before or after in my entire career. In fact, when I asked Mr. Manolic whether he wished to authorise the text, I couldn't have believed in my wildest dreams that in authorising the text from talking to him he -- he could redact my question and his answer, said an angry Dunja Ujevic." And I'd like to ask you the following question: Mr. Manolic, is it true and correct that you asked that a part of the text be expunged? I don't -- it's not important which excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dunja Ujevic would have to prove, first of all, what she's saying. It says -- she says Mr. Manolic became angry. That's not true. Mrs. Dunja Ujevic recorded the talk, so let her bring in the tape. Let's have the tape and then we can see whether there was an interruption or not. So she has no proof or evidence to say what she is doing. That is false testimony. I did not want that portion probably to be included because it was my interview, it wasn't the journalist's interview. I was granting the interview and giving it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. So we can agree that certain -- the interviews in your book are your own interviews in conformity with your interpretation as to how you interpret the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are my interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Let's continue. Just let me see if I'm going too fast. Tell me this, Mr. Manolic, please: In your testimony so far, in your presentation so far --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me where I said what.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: -- you said that the Croats from Banja Luka moved out following appeals from Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you forgot another sentence before that, that under pressure from the Serbian aggression and the appeal by Mr. Boban, that the result was that they moved out of that area. So there were two components whereas you just refer to one component, which is not the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this now Mr. Manolic, please: Omarska, Manjaca, do those names ring a bell? Do they mean anything to you? Do you have any knowledge of those places, and why were they known?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were known because of the crimes. They were known as being camps, and one of my ministers from my government was there, who was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who controlled those camps and who closed them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's general knowledge, it's generally known.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell the Court for the transcript, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Karadzic's camps and prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in them? Who were the inmates, who were the prisoners, ethnically speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly they were Croats and Muslims. Mostly. There were probably others too.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I hope you will agree with me when I say - just give me a yes or no answer - that people were raped, tortured, killed in those camps, abused in various ways. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, and we condemned it at that time and I see no reason for bringing that up now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me this then, please, Mr. Manolic: As an individual, as a human being, I think that it is more logical that the Croats and other non-Serb population, not only the Croats but we're dealing with Croats here, they're essential to us, they moved out of those areas because of the pogrom they were exposed to.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that to begin with. The very fact that you left out. I said that it was under the Serb aggression that they left the area and moved out. The other problem arose with the appeal from Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, this is not a debate between you and Defence counsel. You are here to answer questions for the Judges. So look at me. You're becoming a little excited and that's not going to serve any purpose. Defence counsel asked you a question about Omarska camp, so give your answer calmly to us. Please proceed, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I just have one more question in that regard.
