Tell me, please, Mr. Manolic, do you consider that the Croats should have stayed on and waited for them to shut them up in camps or kill them, or was it more opportune for them to leave?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime conditions, people say -- try and save their skins and groups try and save their skins in different ways. Some people flee, leave all their property, because you have to save your life.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Manolic. Now let's move forward. In one of the statements you made today during your testimony, you said that the late President Tudjman replaced Mr. Boban on the eve of the Washington Agreement because he was in favour of the war option previously. You also said that on the side of Alija Izetbegovic there were also individuals who advocated the war option, who were in favour of war and who had to be replaced and dismissed. Is that true and correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You couldn't have a clash or conflict with people just thinking one thing. You had to have two parties to a conflict. A conflict always involves two or more sides. That's logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, then, please, Mr. Manolic, whether you know who the people were who advocated the war option on Alija Izetbegovic's side.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that now. Perhaps I knew them at the time, but I've quite forgotten them now. But I'm sure you will able to find them in the different documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether he actually replaced any of those people, any of those individuals who were in favour of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were changes, both in the party and in the government structures, but what he did I really can't say, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Let's move on. Tell me this, please, Mr. Manolic, you also said during your testimony that Mr. Izetbegovic uttered the well-known sentence when he said this is not our war and that he was talking about the sending out of Bosniaks to the Yugoslav People's Army at that point in time. Is that correct? Did I understand you correctly and remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when did you read that statement of his, that sentence as uttered by him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was bandied about quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. Where did you read it exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that. There were hundreds of meetings, lots of material, lots of erroneous, incorrect, sometimes truthful reports and reporting. I really can't say where I first heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Then tell me this, please: Would you agree with me if I were to put it to you that Mr. Kljuic was -- had better knowledge of the circumstances in Bosnia and Herzegovina than you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, because he lived there, he lived in that environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, then, that Mr. Kljuic had better knowledge of what Mr. Izetbegovic actually said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I allow for that possibility too. Now, what it was that he knew and quoted is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic -- and Your Honours, yesterday we had some polemics over this, whether we could show the witness what Mr. Kljuic said. I think that would be in order now, so I'm going to tell the witness that Mr. Kljuic in his statement said that the dissatisfaction and revolt among the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was caused by the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic said this is not our war at a point in time when the Croats were being attacked, not only in the Republic of Croatia but there were also attacks by the Serb aggressor in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the Croatian people were revolted because of that because they thought that the government in Sarajevo would not be able to protect and defend them. Do you allow that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for the fact that they felt insecure, just as there was in any armed conflict. Now, whether what Kljuic said was exactly correct, I don't know. I think we could believe him. I think we could take his statement to be truthful since he was in a position to know, both as a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a man who lived over there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you this, Mr. Manolic: Over the past few days during your testimony we read or, rather, the Prosecutor read out within the scope of 3112 document, records from the national Security Council and Defence Council of the 2nd of July, '73 [as interpreted], he read out a letter by John Major, British Prime Minister, to the foreign minister. During your testimony linked to that letter told us here that you doubted its authenticity, and you explained why. Now, can you tell me whether and when you doubted the authenticity of that letter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no discussion about the letter later on at that meeting, at that session, and I was allowed to have my doubts or I could accept that it was an original authentic letter by the signatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to have shown Prosecution Exhibit number 503112. ERN page 01866481. P 03112. I see it's a problem. P as in Peter. Could we have ERN number 01866481. If possible, could we now zoom on the last passage in that -- on that page. Yes, that's it. This is an excerpt that you see in front of it, and it says: "Fourthly ..." It's an excerpt which pertains to your comment on that letter. It says: "Fourthly, there is an issue of this document. Without that document it would have been clear to me the English policy and the French policy in the territory of former Yugoslavia. But just so you know, the English policy is drawing you and me into a third Yugoslavia, and I don't wish to go to the third Yugoslavia. As long as I have this understanding, that the English policy is taking this direction, then I will be against this English policy." Please tell me, Mr. Manolic, are these your words?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: It seems to me, as I look at this text, that you are referring to this letter and drawing some conclusions from it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say so. However, you didn't read out everything. You didn't read all the passage, so now you have me all perplexed whether I was referring to that particular document, that letter right then, or something completely unrelated to that. I don't think it would be that difficult to read out all of the passages where I speak of item 1, 2, 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only item 4 pertains to this particular letter. I can show the entire text, but only this passage pertains to this document, and that was the only document presented at that session, the document pertaining to the English policy. Now, my last question before my client takes over. Tell me, please, at the time while you were chief of security services in the Republic of Croatia, you told us that it was the office for the protection of constitutional order within the presidential office, did your offices also deal with the security in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Was it within their scope of work, the state of security in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At least not during my term. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour, but before my client takes over, could the registry please show us document PD 00477 -- 5D 00477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The registry has 20 minutes to prepare this document. I believe that that should be sufficient time. We now have our break, and we will come back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The Prosecutor has told us he needs at least 20 minutes for redirect. Mr. Coric, you have until 1.25. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, I'm Valentin Coric, the accused. To the last question put to you by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, you said that in 1992, which was during the time that you held the most responsible posts in Croatia in this field, the Croatian security services did not work in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That wasn't within their scope of duties. The document that the Defence counsel put to you will prove something else. I'm not asking for your response, but would you please read out the heading of that document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is in front of me, what you are implying about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: It says Ministry of -- Republic of Croatia Ministry of the Interior, Service for Protection of Constitutional Order. The date is 15th of October, 1992, strictly confidential, reproduction prohibited, and it says here: "Acting assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Marijan Benko." Subject is, "The activity of the security service of HOS and a group for the so-called quiet liquidation." Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Could we now see the last page, which is page 5, where, in addition to the signature, we will see, where it says assistant minister, Smiljan Reljic, and a signature. On the left side it says forwarded to the head of the office for protection for ZUP of RH, Mr. Manolic, and then minister of the interior of RH, Mr. Jarnjak, and then deputy minister of the interior, Mr. Tomljenovic. The next person is assistant minister of defence of the RH security and information service, Mr. Perkovic. Acting assistant minister of the interior of the RH, Mr. Benko. And the last item is SZUP, I and V department. Is that what it says there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: My first question: Do you know those persons whose names I just read out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: At that time in 1992 and 1993, did you have occasional or frequent meetings with these persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very occasional, and with some of them I never met at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasional meetings with Mr. Josip Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. I would meet more often with the minister of the interior, Jarnjak, and his assistant mentioned here, Mr. -- assistant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Benko?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Benko, rather his boss who was assistant minister, Reljic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Reljic. He was the head of SZUP?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Assistant minister but the first man of SZUP in Croatia. Did you ever have joint meetings with these people?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never joint meetings but we would have individual contact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Did these people send you reports on any specific questions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, but yes, they would send reports.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move from this document. We'll get back to it a bit later. In 1992, did you meet with any person working in the services, any one's services, that is to say services of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or Krajina from the territory of Herceg-Bosna -- or, rather, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but if you were to give me some names, I can give you a better reply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: No, I'm quite happy with your reply. Did you ever exchange information between the services of two countries, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know at which level and in which form.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: At your level, the information reaching you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean written information or verbal information? I don't think that I exchanged any written information. If you have any evidence to the contrary, then would you please present it to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: No. Since my time is limited, we need to be as specific as possible. Based on this document, we could see that the first men of SZUP, which is the service for protection of constitutional order, provided to you the most important information.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that reached him. He would provide it to me or directly to the president, because he also had direct communication with the president.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: All right. We can conclude with this and we can move on to something else. The HOS. The first day of your evidence you spoke about the HOS as one of the most extreme formations of the Croatian Party of Rights. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Should I elaborate for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: No, because I don't have the time. Otherwise, very gladly because you know much more about this than I do and I would gladly know as much as you do. What was the name of the first -- the most top ranked person within the HOS?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was Kraljevic, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And who was the top HOS man in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paraga and then Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Was Blaz Kraljevic answerable to Paraga?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I don't know about their internal relations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps whether Alija Izetbegovic at that time accepted the HOS as a legal military formation within the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina? When I say "the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina," I am referring to the same structure that exists in Croatia; the Ministry of Defence, police, and so on. There was a similar structure in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Was the HOS accepted there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that with certainty, but I think that at that time they looked favourably upon each other, favourably, but I have nothing to corroborate this with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only elaborate on consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the HOS commander in Bosnia-Herzegovina had the rank of general?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: General Blaz Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that and I don't know who inducted him into general.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I asked you. It was Alija Izetbegovic who gave him that rank?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but those are their internal relations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but you know that you and I don't know each other so we can't speak of relations between you and me, we can only speak of relations between other people. Do you know that Blaz Kraljevic, in his cooperation with the BH army and with Alija Izetbegovic considered the HVO an illegal military formation at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that with certainty what relations existed there. All I know is the tragedy which took place in the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, but please let me lead this cross-examination. I hope that you know that the HOS was composed of soldiers of almost all ethnicities; Muslims, Croats and Serbs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that because I don't know that. By don't think that there were Serbs within that structure. Maybe you know better than I do, in which case I'm not going to take issue with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: I think that we had some evidence about that and when the time comes we can adduce more evidence about this. Let us move on. Do you know that Blaz Kraljevic, with the support of the BH army, in 1992 prepared an ultimatum to the HVO about disbanding the HVO? This was happening around June and this meeting was held in Mostar. Have you heard of this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go back to the document. I'm going to read only a portion of it even though the document is six pages long. So the subject was the activity of the HOS security service and a group for a so-called quiet liquidation. This is in reference to a letter number such-and-such of the SIS.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SIS of what, of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: There existed only the SIS of the HVO. Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have the SIS. And this deals with the SIS of the Republic of Croatia. This is why I asked you about some of the top people within this service. I'm now reading the documents: "Through operative methods and the means of SZUP we were unable to confirm the SIS information that at the level of the HOS for Dalmatia a security service was supposed to be established or, rather, a group for quiet liquidation."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: This is a document that you were supposed to receive. At least, that's what it says there. This was a strictly confidential document. Any reproduction was prohibited. That is to say it was available only to the very few. As far as I know, we did not receive this document from the Prosecution. This wasn't disclosed by them, no. We received it from the MUP of Croatia, and this is where they can find it. I will now continue reading the document: "However, such a service or such a group, based on the reports of reliable sources of SZUP, is active in the territory of Herzegovina and partially in the territory of the Republic of Croatia, which in accordance with the HOS structure, are subordinated to the War Staff of the HOS for Herzegovina from Ljubusko. In addition, in the territory of Ploce --" I'm not going to read this portion. Let me now abbreviate this. The HOS security service responsible for Herzegovina and the territory of Croatian municipalities subordinated to the War Staff for Herzegovina was established in late February, 1992. It intensified its activity starting in late April, from which time it became active from the HOS barracks in Dretelj near Capljina. Within it are the military police of the HOS and the secret service which are, and especially the latter one, tasked with creating the so-called groups for quiet liquidation, or silent liquidation. This is page 2. I think that you had a similar situation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "similar situation." The fact is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me complete.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Don't interrupt me. I'm examining you here. With all due respect to your age and everything else. So we had the following situation in Herzegovina, or in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Namely, we had several armies, several security services, several military police, several secret service. What I read out, does it confirm --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that. Don't try to get me to talk about things that I am not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: We're analysing this document together now. First I am putting it to you --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, but you are stating that there were several armies, several security services, intelligence services. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: You don't want to know that. Had you listened to me carefully, you would have known, but you are refusing to know this. This is stated in a document that you refused, Mr. Manolic. You were supposed to read this document and take certain steps based on this document. I'd like to continue now. The task of the secret police - this is referring to the HOS secret police - is defined as counter-espionage, intelligence work in relation to the leadership and units of the HVO and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, uncovering of the fifth columnists, monitoring of suspicious persons, and uncovering of hidden activists of the Serbian Democratic Party by -- in addition to uncovering such persons, this service was also tasked with organising their arrest, investigation, and possible liquidation. The commander of the HOS secret police in Dretelj was Mirsad Muminagic, known as Tadija, from Struge. I'm going to skip over some text. He personally was subordinated to Blaz Kraljevic, HOS commander, with whom he met regularly in the premises of the staff in Ljubusko. Now my comment. Mirsad Muminagic, judging by his name, to what ethnic community does he belong? And he was the head of the HOS secret service.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely he's a Muslim, but I don't see why you're asking me that. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: It is up to the Bench to assess this, not up to you. Now I'm continuing with the reading of this report that was sent to you, Mr. Manolic. "The information of the SZUP in relation to the secret activity of the HOS service indicates that its members committed at least 12 liquidations of persons of Serb ethnicity." Then it goes on to discuss some persons. I don't want to reveal their names, places of their execution, their bodily remains, corpses that were burned, their positions and so on, and I'm skipping over to page 3. Further on: "The abductions and liquidations were committed pursuant to the order of Mirsad Muminagic, the commander of the secret police. The executioners are persons currently unknown to the SZUP except that they were members of the HOS. They would come from other places especially in order to carry out these tasks. They would come from Mostar, Stolac, and other places in order to reduce the possibility of them being identified." Now I would like to read the following passage, also on page 3: "Following the death of Blaz Kraljevic, members of the HOS secret police carried out an investigation of this event. They found witnesses, questioned them, and took statements from them." I'm now moving to page 4. "This activity was carried out under the order of the so-called main inspector of the HOS, Mile Dedakovic aka Jastreb, who temporarily took over the command of HOS in Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please give me the year, at least the year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: This is around September of 1992. Who is Dedakovic, Mile Dedakovic, called Jastreb? We saw his position within the HOS. What was he prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer of the JNA who sometime in September of 1991 crossed over into Croatian army. At the time he was sent to the front in Vukovar and there at the front he didn't conduct himself honourably, following which he had a conflict, and we started, instituted proceedings against him. There was a police investigation against him, and I think that after that he went to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: "Mile Dedakovic called Jastreb took over temporary command over HOS in Herzegovina. Dedakovic, based on the information gathered, issued an order that Primorac Ivica, former vice-commander of HOS, be placed under surveillance." Have you ever met Mr. Primorac?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I heard of him. I might have heard of him at certain meetings, I might have come across him, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: To read on: "Stojic Bruno, the commissioner for defence of the Herceg-Bosna community ..." as is said in the text here, and you met him, he's sitting here?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: And Valentin Coric, the commander of the military police department of the HVO. They were also included on the list for liquidation. I'm not going to read the text further although there are other individuals as well. But to go back to the commander of the secret police, Muminagic Mirsad, and I'm reading on: "In connection with the above it is important to note that Muminagic Mirsad, according to information gained by SZUP, joined HOS pursuant to instructions from Dzemal Najetovic, the former officer of the security services of the Yugoslav People's Army, who at the time was performing the function of commander of the Territorial Defence unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina (the Muslim one) in a place called Jasenica in Capljina municipality. We identified Muminagic earlier on as an operative of the security service of the Yugoslav army in Capljina." And to read on and finish the text, page 4: "Among the members of the HOS units in our territory, there are several individuals who have already shown themselves to be the perpetrators of terrorist acts (mining facilities and property, shoot-ups in apartments and others) and among them could be a recruited possible members of groups for silent liquidation." That concludes my reading of that passage, and I now have a few questions to ask you about that. In interstate communication, for example in peacetime, as we are now, if the service of a country were to receive a piece of information of this kind, wouldn't it be logical that that information be sent out via Interpol to the country whose citizens are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in normal conditions, that would be normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, I have checked - and others are free to check this out too - this information none of us received, none of us in the HVO security service. Had we received it, we would have found it in some archive. Can you believe that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can believe that, but I think that the assistant defence minister had intensive contacts with Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you that at that time, 1992, I was the number one man of SIS for a time and also commander of the military police, and at this time I was head of the military police administration, and I never received any report to that effect. Can you believe me if I tell you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to believe you, because you're the witness and I have no other proof or evidence. But I think that the Court should be told who and what HOS is, the H-O-S, that you're talking about, because I think that the leaders of that -- of the HOS was in Zagreb, in Croatia, whereas these were branches of it. And I'm hearing now for the first time that Dedakovic was, for instance, in Bosnia-Herzegovina in HOS. But the road traversed was this: When we completed the police investigation of Dedakovic, because we had suspicions, well-founded suspicions where he was concerned, I think that after that, when he left prison, that he joined HOS, HOS Zagreb with Paraga and Djapic, and that it was they who sent him to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So our service had to tackle HOS, and I myself, and up to the present day the vestiges of HOS.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but you're taking up my time. I just have two more questions, Your Honour. The first question is this: I did not read out four or five names of men who were members of the Croatian army who were involved in this operation, and since the document has now become public to all of us, were those people prosecuted in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who you mean. If you give me the names, I'll be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll read the names out, then. They are as follows --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prosecuted Paraga and some people around Paraga.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Would you just leave me enough time to read this out. In preparing these activities, Milicevic Damir, commander of the HOS military police, took part. He was a policeman in Capljina. Milicevic Stjepan, commander of the Metkovici police.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of those names. I've never heard of them or the proceedings. There were no legal proceedings initiated against them in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to ask you. My last question now, Mr. Manolic. Now, the story around this document shows and proves -- does it show and prove what kind of criminal enterprise it was between the people in Croatia and Herceg-Bosna for which we are being held accountable? Would that be logical?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during these proceedings, during the case and trial, you'll be able to establish that. I told you that I cannot enter into that. When you go to Bosnia-Herzegovina -- I don't know you personally. We never had any personal contacts, and you occupied prominent positions in that area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, don't involve me in things I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, from what you've just said leads me to make one more observation and ask a question. Listening to you over the past few days, I cannot believe that you were so courageous us to make assessments and evaluations about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina with so little knowledge, so I'm not surprised that you don't know me at all. I was a lower ranking officer, but nevertheless I was minister of the MUP of Herceg-Bosna, I was member of the Presidency of the presidential council, I was minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I am astounded in noting that you are brave enough to speak out on such -- such important questions, fateful to the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, without that knowledge. Thank you. You needn't answer that question. ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just a short question that I have following on from what's just been said and a number of questions raised by Mr. Coric. When you received the letter, what did you do? Did you put it in a drawer or did you pass it on to the people that should have reacted and apprehended those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president was informed of that letter. As can be seen, the letter was sent to all high personages who were supposed to take steps; to everyone ranging from Mr. Reljic and all the others mentioned here. Now, what they actually did, what action they took, I don't know because I never received any feedback information about that. But generally speaking, I think that the information was correct. And this testimony of Benko's was objective and can be believed, is believable. Now, what I wanted to make clear to this Honourable Trial Chamber is how HOS was organised. HOS was an ultra-Nazi organisation during that period of time which stood up to and worked to topple the constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia, and now we can see that it had strong roots or tentacles in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. It was an organisation that was of that nature. We in Croatia did not carry out any of the liquidations he was talking about. What we did was to initiate legal proceedings against the main people like Paraga. The court acquitted Paraga to begin with as the organiser of these paramilitary operations, but then the court, the Supreme Court, ruled that they were paramilitary formations, HOS formations, belonging to a political party, which was something that could not be tolerated. So until they joined up with the regular units of the Croatian army, we considered them to be paramilitary formations and then we acted accordingly towards them as illegal formations and we took proceedings both in courts of law and through the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to have a follow-up question to the President Antonetti about your obligations and tasks in your office. Before the break we have listened to Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, who is the counsel for Valentin Coric, and she mentioned that you were the chief of the secret services in Croatia. I do not find now this line, but it was about ten minutes before we -- before our break. So my question is in a way a follow-up question, that what were your real responsibilities in your office? Did you -- did you have operational responsibilities and tasks? Did you coordinate the secret services, or was it rather in a way in the presidential office to -- to collect the information and give it to the president, of course which also implied certain operational activities? So I would like to ask you what were your area of responsibilities in your office there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My remit or area of responsibility was contained in the decision of the president to establish that office in the first place. There was stipulated what my responsibilities were and what the authorisations of the department were, to collect, supply, and coordinate material and give it to the president of the republic. So nothing took place without the president having been informed about it. Or, if I considered that a certain piece of information was of no interest or was foul play on somebody's part, then I didn't send it on to the president. But in addition to that, we must also know that the president had an advisor for national security, and that advisor for national security also worked in that area, that is to say collecting and amassing information, and if there was any need to intervene on the basis of the knowledge and reports received, he could do that. The services within the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the protection of the state order, the SIS heads also collected information and would send that information out to their ministers, who could react, and this information was either sent on or not to the presidential office. I don't know if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Manolic, a few follow-up questions following from the cross-examination. I just want to start, and we probably won't have the time to pull up all of these documents. I will read some excerpts from them, some of them that were put to you by the Defence. They can be translated to you. If it becomes absolutely necessary, we can pull some of them up on the screen. But counsel for Mr. Petkovic showed you an article, an interview from Globus on the 7th of November, 1997. Let me just read to you the very beginning of your answer given at that time, and then I'll have a question for you about that. "I criticised Tudjman the most for his policy towards the Republic Herceg-Bosna. I have been the biggest opponent of the establishment of the Republic Herceg-Bosna in the HDZ at the time and the time showed that, from a strategic point of view, I was right and that was the biggest pleasure for me and my party, that time verified us." Now, sir, is that statement consistent with the criticisms and differences that you had with Tudjman, Susak, and others that you have told the Judges about these last three and a half days?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that would be correct. I don't know see any difference there. If there are any differences during the first day of my testimony and later on in the cross-examination, well, we would have to determine what was different so that we can explain, whether it was through a memory lapse, intentional, unintentional. But I stand by the text as a whole, and all the texts that I published here. I have no dilemma on that score, no queries, quandaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, our time is limited so let me try to move forward fairly quickly. Ongoing questions about Karadjordjevo. Let me ask you this, sir: Is it correct to say that one can also get confirmation of the existence in terms of the meeting by the conduct that takes place following a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, time -- time may be short, but I'm going to ask that Mr. Scott not lead the witness during redirect examination. And it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, it does not call for any speculation. It's a general proposition of human behaviour. Can one draw --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's beyond the scope of this gentleman's expertise. He's not a psychiatrist or a psychologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with psychologists. This is a question of human conduct and someone who has been a senior official, attended many meetings, can talk about whether conduct following a meeting tends to confirm what happened at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer, but to repeat that I stand by my previous statements. You just read out a statement that I don't have in front of me right this minute, and I don't know how to phrase my position, but if you were to put me -- put it on the screen for me, I'd be able to give you my position right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... particular article you wrote now. Let me restate my question, and I'm sorry, I know you're tired. Let me repeat my question. Can you tell us, sir, in your experience is it often the case that one can gain information about what happens at a meeting by seeing and observing the conduct that takes place after such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. Now we're talking -- who are we talking about in general? I think this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Human behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think this is improper rebuttal testimony. He had ample opportunity to ask what he observed after the meeting. That's testimony, those would be facts, then it would be up to the Trial Chamber to draw conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand Mr. Scott quite clearly. Was it possible to confirm only which took place at an official meeting, which was also recorded and transcripts, or was it possible to obtain information elsewhere? Yes, certainly information was also obtained elsewhere; in the corridors and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said one of the things that President Tudjman reported when he came back from Karadjordjevo, that the topic of Kosovo was discussed. And can you confirm to the Judges again that, after that meeting, in fact Croatia stopped its radio broadcast into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I said correctly that that programme was terminated based on direct proposal of the president. And you can call Mr. Vrdoljak here to testify. At the time he was the director of the Zagreb TV. But the fact is that that programme was terminated, and I link it to the fact that that was a concession to Milosevic in relation to Kosovo, because he said that Kosovo was an internal problem of the state of Serbia. I think that's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you also said, and whatever the other disagreements might be, that the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was at least discussed, if not agreed, as reported by Franjo Tudjman. Can you confirm, sir, that what you've told us, that following Karadjordjevo, President Tudjman set up a group that was supposed to prepare maps and demarcations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, is this new testimony or is this rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In response to the questions raised on cross-examination, Your Honour. Specifically -- many counsel went on and on about whether Karadjordjevo happened or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is improper rebuttal then, because the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, your redirect questions have to be based on what was covered during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please tell us, on which parts of cross-examination do you base this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Defence counsel have continued to question whether any meeting at Karadjordjevo occurred, or what happened there, what the terms of any agreement were. I'm coming back to respond specifically to those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic. In theory, when it comes to additional questions, to redirect, there is no right to intervene. Please go ahead, Ms. Alaburic. And following that, we will have to stop with these interventions because if you all keep rising, there will be no time for the Prosecutor to complete their questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our questions did pertain to Karadjordjevo but the topic of the work of this commission doesn't relate only to the meeting in Karadjordjevo, because before and after that at the meetings between the presidents of all six republics of the former Yugoslavia, they discussed the territorial delineations, and none of the questions of Defence pertained to the work of these commissions which were established in all republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me repeat my question to you. Was it -- can you confirm to the Judges again that following President Tudjman coming back from Karadjordjevo, was a group established for the purpose of preparing maps and demarcations of territory? That's really fairly -- if you don't know, if you don't remember, but --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the central issue that this Honourable Chamber has to rule on is the role of President Tudjman in the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The agreement that he had with Milosevic is something that he conveyed to us in principle. He told us in principle, we agreed that the area in -- territory in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia will be divided based on our agreement. The implementation and the operations that ensued was a confirmation in principle of that agreement. He delegated it to some people, to a group of people in Croatia, really prominent people in Croatia, academician --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question that was put to you required you to say whether, after he came back, a commission for maps was established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Academician Bilandzic, who was a member of the commission, said that on the 10th of March, or perhaps 10th of April, I'm not sure, he was called by President Tudjman, who told him, "I'm hereby establishing a team of experts -" that's what he called it, a team of experts - "comprising yourself -" and his name was -- rather, there were another three men there as well, but all prominent, respectable figures in Croatian politics; a current judge on the Constitutional Court, a well-known lawyer was also a member of that commission. And no need for me to go into detail, these are publicly known facts. So this was an expert commission which was supposed to prepare the implementation of this agreement in principle, to implement it with all the appropriate documents. Then on the Serbian side Milosevic also established an expert team which worked jointly on the implementation of this agreement in principle with Milosevic. This is all that I can tell you. This is what I eyewitnessed as a protagonist in Croatian politics. As for the other questions involving Herceg-Bosna and all the other events, I think that you need to further discuss it with these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, the witness has now answered your question about the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving next to the -- very, very briefly to the Graz Agreement. Can you just simply tell the Judges -- I just want, if you know, if you can give us some final assistance on that, do you know whether the international community immediately rejected the Graz Agreement as a bilateral agreement inconsistent with the international peace negotiations that were taking place at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you may caution me, I apologise, but this is truly a leading question. Even though you banned us from intervening, I couldn't refrain on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, if you phrase it this way --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this is a leading question. I already spoke about this. I already gave my position on this. It's just that Mr. Scott wants me to reiterate this. He believes it to be significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On redirect, you have to -- you have to base it -- base your questions on what was asked during cross-examination. You cannot bring in any other issues. Mr. Scott, if you are putting this question. It has to rely on what the witness said during cross-examination. Do you have any reference? Can you point us to a specific portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I cannot take you to a page in the transcript at this time. I have not had time to go back to study the transcript and give you a page and line number, of course not. If the Chamber does not recall Defence questions about the Graz Agreement the last day and a half, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, you have to withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Am I to understand then, Your Honour, for the future, that for redirect purposes, that we will need to cite the page and line number of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it be that rigid, but he must say, You were asked a question by the Defence ... and at least to show that it is in rebuttal not new information. If the gentleman forgot to ask it before, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not. Your Honour, the question was put --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he wants to ask it again for the second time, it's not rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, multiple Defence counsel, and I'm sorry, I cannot go back to the transcript now and find all the references to the Defence questioning about Graz, but I submit to you they were considerable. And the implication was either it didn't occur or that what happened there -- or that what happened there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But, Mr. Scott, there certainly had to be questions to which the witness gave answers that you were not satisfied with, and this is why you noted this down that you needed to cover this in redirect. So where does the problem lie? What did you see that you objected to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought we had this witness here and, based on all the questions that had been put to him about Graz, if he can assist the Chamber further to clarify what happened after Graz, I thought I would ask him. And to assist you, in the questions that were raised by the Defence, a suggestion that it was either inconsistent or consistent with other peace processes, I would ask the witness to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But before the Graz Agreement -- or, rather, after the Graz Agreement, after the Graz Agreement, based on what you saw yourself, can you tell us what happened following that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What happened following that was that the armed conflict between Croats and Bosnian Serbs ended, that is to say between Croats and Karadzic. That was the result of that agreement. I personally didn't see the text of the agreement, but those were the results, the consequences; that the armed conflict between the Croats and Bosnian Serbs ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for -- just for the record, I want to make sure that we're very clear, at least on the part of the Defence. We maintain that there was no agreement. We've never objected to there being a meeting. And there's extensive discussion on this. In fact, Mr. Kljuic, who is the gentleman's friend, indicated that he didn't believe that anything occurred as far as an agreement at this Graz meeting, so we object to the characterisation as there being an agreement. A meeting? Not a problem, we discussed that. Whether the internationals agreed or disagreed, that's a separate issue. But I want to make sure that we're clear that we at no time concede that there was an agreement in Graz.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fine. I understand that position, Your Honour. And just like my previous question, it is a fair -- it is fair for the Judges to be informed -- if their dispute, as you've just heard, there is a no agreement, but if there is conduct following a meeting that implies or suggests that there was a meeting, then the Chamber should be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that's for direct examination, not for rebuttal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going at it again. You're arguing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. My apology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please settle down. In principle, when there is an agreement, generally there tends to be a document that is signed. If we don't have a signed document, then we can say that it was only a meeting. Mr. Manolic, following that meeting which was held, in your judgement the consequence of that meeting was that the conflict between Serbs and Croats ended; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the signed agreement or the signed document didn't exist; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether there existed a signed document, I think, though, that there was a statement given. Whether there was a heading saying "agreement" is something that is disputed, but I think that it can be clarified through various documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, very briefly. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Mr. Manolic, following that agreement, we liberated both the right and the left bank of Mostar for the length of 30 kilometres in -- in June. So how can you say that the conflict between Serbs and Croats stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the purpose of that agreement, to end the conflict between Serbs and Croats in that area. And this is what transpired later on. Maybe in June there still existed a conflict, but not later on. There was no conflict with Karadzic later on. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] What about Bosanski Brod? What about Posavina? Where did you live at the time I have to wonder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, your objection was recorded. Mr. Scott, have you concluded with this or not? Because we should have ended five minutes ago and there is another trial which is scheduled to begin after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I appreciate that and I will shorten my questions. Unfortunately, for all the interventions, we haven't been able to get very far, but that's the reality, I understand. Let me just look, Your Honour. If I can ask two or three questions. If I can just look at my outline, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony yesterday, you said at one point in answer to questions from the Defence, you used -- part of your answer was that Tudjman engaged in a quote - and this was your phrase, it was at page -- at least, as of yesterday. I know sometimes the page numbering changes. Page 28, at line 13, you said Tudjman engaged in a "dual policy." Now, can you explain to the Judges, when you say "dual policy" what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mere fact that he acknowledged or recognised the borders of the republics which came to be after the break-up of Yugoslavia, he acknowledged this publicly and then, on the other hand, he and Milosevic established expert groups that were to partition that area. This is where you see the gap, the contradiction between his words and his deeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My final question: On the issue of provision, Croatia's provision of arms or supplies to the Muslims, which again was repeatedly asked and also reflected in a number of Defence exhibits, do you know, can you tell the Chamber, do you know whether any of these arms were actually delivered; and if so, where they were delivered?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether it was delivered. However, the document that was put to us shows that this materiel was there. Whether it was one shipment or multiple shipments, that's irrelevant now. And I think that that's the issue where the Defence makes strategic mistakes, because they are drawing Croatia into new troubles which are troubles with embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: With all due respect, the witness must be instructed to respond to the question and leave it at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just this last response, for the record, shows that the gentleman here is with his own personal agenda. His agenda is to smear Mr. Tudjman and to smear everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that comment right there is objectionable. Mr. Karnavas has no business getting up and slandering this witness in front of this witness and accusing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Manolic. Mr. Manolic, the question was quite specific. The Prosecutor asked you whether you knew whether the weapons were delivered; and if so, where. So the question was quite specific.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I don't know whether it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you don't know that. You just said I saw a document which -- all right. The question was directed to you personally, whether you knew about the shipment of arms from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you say to that "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no knowledge about the arms being delivered. I can just state what was written in that document, that was requested, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up on that and one final question: Can you tell the Judges, sir, were there areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, specifically talking about larger area, Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there areas outside the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna where Muslims and Croats fought together against the Serbs throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to be quite specific there. If you are referring to six or, rather, three provinces, then yes, that area is quite well defined, but in other periods of times and in other discussions the issue was quite different, or the situation was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the interests of time and -- Mr. Manolic, I'll conclude there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Manolic, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you for coming here. You've testified here for several days. This was no small feat for you. It was quite a lengthy testimony. So I wish you a safe trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, very quickly. Mr. Scott, as for our schedule for next week, if I understood you well, we have two witnesses scheduled. One is supposed to testify on Monday and Tuesday and the other one on Wednesday and Thursday. As for the first witness, you foresaw that the examination-in-chief would last three and a half hours and for the second witness five hours. Is that correct? Do you think that you can comply with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, beyond that, the Prosecution will be making an application and makes an oral at this time - we'll be providing this material to the Defence today - to offer as 92 bis evidence the testimony of Stipe Mesic from the Blaskic case, which is our view that the testimony of Mr. Blaskic -- President Blaskic in the -- excuse me: President Mesic in the Blaskic case -- it's late in the day -- is corroboration of the testimony that the Court has received from Mr. Manolic and we will -- we are by this, by what I'm saying now, applying that the Chamber receive that evidence under Rule 92 bis, and we'll provide that to the Chamber today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have two unrelated matters. So I am not going to argue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. So there's this oral request pursuant to Rule 92 bis and Mr. Mesic's testimony in the Blaskic case. Now, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not going to respond to that oral request, Your Honour, but I have two oral requests myself. One is with respect to the joint response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. With respect to the oral motion, the Defence will also state its views. So you must state your position. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we oppose. We want Mr. Mesic here. We believe Mr. Mesic should be subjected to proper cross-examination in open public, in open -- in open. And we want -- and I should add that after he testified, because first time he came he took part of the archive and brought it here, then after he testified it was open, so we have more material, more documents that were not available at the time he testified, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I understand that on behalf of the Defence you would like him to appear. And everybody agrees, do they?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Now -- two other points. This joint response with respect to the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice is due today at 4.00. We have it prepared, but because we've been working rather hard with this last witness, I would ask leave to file it on Monday so I could double-check it and perhaps even make it a little bit tighter, but we do have it but I would appreciate if we could have that to be -- And then the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- I'm making an oral application for the Trial Chamber to provide me with OLAD's response to my request to have my client use a computer. I know a decision with a dissent was issued. I never received that memo. OLAD will not turn it over to me without a request from the -- from the Chamber or without a decision from the Chamber, so I would most -- I wish to file a leave for certification to appeal that, Your Honour, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is five minutes past 2.00. I apologise to the interpreters for having kept them for this additional work. I wish everyone a very good weekend and we reconvene on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
